articles.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a time-critical neurological emergency associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Data on its burden and predictors among patients with established epilepsy presenting to the emergency department (ED) remain limited, particularly in Asian settings. This study aimed to determine the incidence of SE, its association with in-hospital mortality, and its predictors. This multicentre prospective observational study was conducted across 34 public hospitals in Malaysia. Epilepsy patients presenting to the ED with seizures were recruited using convenience sampling. The primary endpoints were SE and in-hospital mortality. Predictors were identified using logistic regression analysis. A total of 521 patients were included, of whom 119 (22.8%) had SE. In-hospital mortality rate was 3.5%. SE was independently associated with mortality (aOR 9.17, 95% CI 3.14-26.78; p < 0.01), along with prior ischaemic stroke (aOR 5.75, 95% CI 2.13-15.56; p = 0.01). Independent predictors of SE included age ≥ 60 years (aOR 1.79, 95% CI 1.03-3.11, p = 0.04), hyperglycaemia (aOR 2.08, 95% CI 1.10-3.91, p = 0.02), hypocalcaemia (aOR 2.50, 95% CI 1.06-5.90, p = 0.04), central nervous system infections (aOR 7.80, 95% CI 2.80-21.78, p < 0.01), and phenytoin use (aOR 1.98, 95% CI 1.16-3.37, p = 0.01). SE occurred in nearly one-quarter of epilepsy patients presenting to the ED and was strongly associated with increased in-hospital mortality. These findings may assist clinicians in identifying patients at increased risk of SE and support early risk stratification and appropriate monitoring, particularly among older patients and those presenting with metabolic abnormalities or suspected CNS infection.

articles.title: Frailty stratification in the emergency department using the triage frailty and comorbidity tool.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: Frailty is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of adverse outcomes and resource use in the Emergency Department (ED), yet pragmatic, scalable strategies for timely identification and management are lacking. We evaluated a workflow-compatible frailty stratification model by embedding the Triage Frailty and Comorbidity (TFC) Tool into routine triage for low-acuity patients. We conducted a multicentre observational study in two Italian EDs. Adult patients triaged as Manchester Triage System (MTS) green/blue were eligible. As part of triage completion, nurses completed the TFC Tool; TFC ≥ 5% defined positivity. For TFC-positive patients, the waiting-list order was prioritised within the same MTS category. Primary outcome was time from triage completion to medical evaluation; secondary outcome was hospitalisation. Among 40,568 eligible visits, 1269 (3.1%) were TFC-positive (0.3% in 18-65 years; 9.8% in ≥65 years). In adjusted models, TFC positivity was associated with a + 1.45 (95%CI 1.19-1.70) minute longer triage duration but reduced waiting time to medical evaluation by -15.06 min (95%CI -20.85 to -9.27). Hospitalisation occurred in 19.4% of TFC-positive vs 4.8% of TFC-negative patients; TFC ≥ 5% was independently associated with admission (adjusted OR 1.69, 95%CI 1.43-1.99), and TFC as continuous increased admission odds per 1% point (OR 1.05, 95%CI 1.04-1.06). Routine implementation of the TFC Tool within standard triage was associated with shorter waiting times to medical assessment among vulnerable low-acuity patients, while maintaining acuity-based prioritisation. TFC positivity was also associated with higher odds of hospitalisation.

articles.title: An in vivo assessment of green plasma: The potential hemostatic superiority of a currently discarded blood product.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Approximately 5% of donated plasma has a green appearance, due to elevated ceruloplasmin levels from increased estrogen. These products are currently discarded based on color alone. However, studies have shown improved trauma outcomes from female donors. In an ex vivo study, we recently noted accelerated and increased clot production with green plasma. The purpose of this study was to assess whether these findings could be confirmed in an in vivo animal model of severe hemorrhage. We utilized a well-established rat model of uncontrolled hemorrhage. Following cannulation and anesthesia, 33 rats underwent midline laparotomy followed by excision of 50% of the middle hepatic lobe to induce hemorrhage. After 60 seconds, GREEN (11 rats), standard FEMALE (11), or MALE plasma (11) were infused at a fixed volume of 5 mL. Abdominal cavity blood was collected to evaluate blood loss every 15 minutes for 60 minutes. Deaths occurring before experiment termination were recorded. Rats resuscitated with GREEN plasma had improved shock index compared with FEMALE and MALE at 15 (3.7 vs. 6.2 vs. 10.2; p =0.092), 30 (3.8 vs. 8.2 vs. 6.5; p =0.039), and 60 minutes (3.9 vs. 29.9 vs. 7.1; p =0.015). Mean arterial pressures in GREEN plasma-resuscitated rats were higher at 30 ( p =0.032) and 60 minutes ( p =0.115). Cumulative percent blood volume lost was lower at each time point in those receiving GREEN plasma. Survival to 60 minutes was 100% among GREEN and FEMALE plasma rats but only 64% among MALE resuscitated ones ( p <0.001). Our study demonstrated that green plasma has improved efficacy for reducing bleeding and restoring hemodynamic stability compared with standard plasma in a rodent model of uncontrolled hemorrhage. Combined with our recent ex vivo data noting equivalent (often superior) hemostatic potential compared with standard units, we recommend reintroducing this often-discarded AABB-approved product back into the plasma donor pool.

articles.title: The Geometry of Skin Grafting: Boundary, Seams, and Epithelialization.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Split-thickness skin grafting remains central to definitive wound closure in burn surgery. Although the biology of successful engraftment is well established, less attention has been paid to the geometric and mechanical determinants of graft behavior. Broader grafts often appear more stable and require fewer peripheral fixation points per unit area than surfaces reconstructed from multiple narrow pieces. We propose a clinically grounded framework in which graft geometry defines boundary, interior, seams, and epithelialization gaps. Larger grafts have a lower perimeter-to-area ratio and proportionally more interior, whereas multiple graft pieces create internal seams and additional interface length. These principles apply to unmeshed sheet and meshed grafts. Geometry is not an isolated determinant: central fixation, fibrin adhesion, bolsters, wraps, splints, and negative-pressure wound therapy improve coupling and reduce displacement, but do not remove physical edges, seams, or gap geometry. Seam orientation is clinically consequential. Straight seams should be avoided across flexion creases, joints, and concavities when an alternative is available; unavoidable seams should be reoriented, staggered, interrupted, or constructed nonlinearly. In donor-limited grafting, the objective changes. At comparable high expansion ratios of 3:1 or greater, widely meshed grafts and Meek micrografts distribute epithelial fronts and migration distances differently. This conditional framework translates common operative observations into a vocabulary for planning, teaching, and research. It identifies practical decisions under the surgeon's control and forms testable hypotheses regarding interface length, stabilization, seam orientation, and epithelialization distance.

articles.title: Burn Care in Prisons: Ethical Dilemmas in Correctional Health Care.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Burn injuries among incarcerated individuals represent an underexplored intersection of medical ethics, correctional policy, and health equity. Although scholarship increasingly examines vulnerable groups such as refugees and undocumented patients, incarcerated patients with burn injuries remain largely absent. Dual loyalty-balancing duty to the patient with obligations to the institution or state-creates distinctive challenges that are intensified in burn care, where timely intervention, pain control, rehabilitation, and psychosocial support are critical but often constrained by security protocols and systemic neglect. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus to identify peer-reviewed articles, position statements, and ethical analyses addressing incarcerated healthcare, dual loyalty, and burn treatment (English-language, 2000-2025). A thematic synthesis identified recurring ethical tensions, clinical barriers, and potential frameworks for resolution. Findings highlight a major gap in both literature and professional discourse. Recurrent themes included restricted access to specialized burn centers, compromised informed consent under custodial oversight, inadequate rehabilitative services, and disproportionate suffering linked to institutional neglect. Dual loyalty emerges as a central driver of ethical conflict, often pitting patient dignity against correctional authority. Elevating incarcerated burn care within burn scholarship and advocacy is necessary to uphold standards of care. Explicit attention to dual loyalty can support reforms that preserve patient dignity while maintaining institutional safety, improve outcomes, and reaffirm professional ethical commitments.

articles.title: MicroRNA-Engineered Extracellular Vesicles for Burn Wound Repair: Burn-Specific Design and Translational Perspectives.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Burn wound healing remains a major clinical challenge. This review evaluates microRNA-engineered extracellular vesicles as cell-free therapeutics and proposes a burn-oriented framework linking engineering strategies with burn-specific biological and clinical barriers. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure for studies published between January 1, 2021, and July 4, 2026. Burn-focused and broader wound-healing evidence was reviewed, with relevant earlier seminal studies included when necessary. Upstream parental-cell programming, downstream vesicle modification, and biomaterial-assisted delivery may improve cargo control, targeting, retention, and therapeutic performance. However, much of the available evidence remains derived from non-burn wound models. Burn-specific translation must also address burn depth, eschar, infection, hypoxia, systemic inflammation, inhalation injury, grafting requirements, dose scaling for large burns, repeat application, storage, sterility, and compatibility with debridement and grafting. MicroRNA-engineered extracellular vesicles are a versatile platform for burn wound repair, but clinical translation remains speculative without robust large-animal, infected-burn, grafting, long-term scar, and human safety data.

articles.title: Ethical Challenges of Bioprinted and Lab-Grown Skin Substitutes in Burn Care.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Severe burns continue to impose significant global morbidity and mortality, particularly where surgical and critical-care resources are limited. As survival has improved, attention has shifted toward optimizing reconstruction. Bioprinted and lab-grown skin substitutes-building on advances in tissue engineering, cellular scaffolds, and 3D bioprinting-offer new possibilities for coverage, yet raise ethical, legal, and distributive challenges that remain underexamined in burn care. A narrative review was conducted using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (2010-2025), supplemented by foundational legal and bioethics literature. Sources were selected for conceptual and policy relevance to ownership, consent, commercialization, intellectual property (IP), and equity in regenerative skin technologies. Fifty publications spanning burn surgery, biobanking, organoid governance, IP law, and global health were synthesized inductively. Five major ethical domains emerged: (1) ambiguous ownership and ontological status of hybrid bioprinted tissues; (2) inadequacy of consent processes to address commercialization and downstream uses of patient-derived cells; (3) complex IP environments that may restrict access and clinical innovation; (4) distributive injustice driven by high costs and global resource disparities; and (5) a near absence of empirical ethics research involving burn patients or care teams. Bioprinted and lab-grown skin substitutes could transform burn reconstruction, but current ethical and regulatory frameworks lag behind. Addressing ownership, consent, commercialization, and equity-supported by robust empirical engagement with patients-is essential for responsible integration of these technologies into burn care.

articles.title: Articular compliance and tolerance to residual incongruity after intra-articular fracture: A hypothesis-driven narrative review.
articles.abstract: Residual articular incongruity after intra-articular fracture is widely held to cause post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), yet tolerance of a given step-off differs between joints and between regions of the same joint. Reduction targets are nonetheless expressed as uniform millimetre thresholds, and no tissue-level mechanism has been offered for the variation. The compliance of the osteochondral unit - cartilage thickness, cartilage material properties and subchondral bone stiffness together - modulates tolerance of residual incongruity, and incongruity is more informatively expressed relative to local cartilage thickness than in absolute millimetres. Narrative review with a documented search of PubMed/MEDLINE (inception to 14 October 2026) covering cartilage and subchondral properties of opposing surfaces, experimental and computational studies of articular incongruity, and clinical studies relating residual displacement to outcome. Four searches returned 3928 records, 3579 after deduplication; 54 sources informed the synthesis. This is not a systematic review; reporting follows SANRA. Small, localised contact-stress elevations appear tolerable; step-offs remodel less completely as their height increases; and cumulative contact-stress exposure above a threshold predicts PTOA after tibial plafond fracture. Opposing surfaces differ measurably in cartilage thickness, modulus and subchondral bone thickness, but the direction of the difference reverses between joints and between regions of one joint, so curvature is not a usable proxy for compliance. Clinically, the acetabulum and tibial plafond appear least tolerant, the meniscus-covered tibial plateau more tolerant, and distal radius incongruity predicts radiographic arthrosis more strongly than functional loss. The evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, a contribution of osteochondral compliance; joint-level factors confound the clinical data. We set out a Compliance Framework defining measurable determinants, propose relative incongruity as a testable metric, and state four falsifiable predictions with the designs that would test them. Current joint-specific reduction standards should guide practice until those predictions are tested.

articles.title: Pediatric Musculoskeletal Infections: Who Needs a Tap or MRI? From Kocher to PEMCRC.
articles.abstract: Bacterial musculoskeletal infections (MSKIs), including septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and pyomyositis, are challenging diagnoses to make in pediatric emergency medicine because their presentation frequently overlaps with more common conditions, including transient synovitis, Lyme arthritis, reactive arthritis, and other inflammatory arthritides. While delayed diagnosis may result in significant morbidity, over-testing may expose children to invasive procedures, advanced imaging, sedation, hospitalization, and unnecessary antimicrobial therapy. Pediatric emergency clinicians must therefore balance the competing risks of missed infection and excessive diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Numerous tools exist to aid clinicians, including blood biomarkers-white blood cell (WBC) count, absolute neutrophil count (ANC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT). However, blood biomarkers have limited diagnostic accuracy when used in isolation. To address this limitation, clinical prediction tools that combine laboratory values with clinical features to stratify risk have been developed. In this review, we summarize the data for clinically available biomarkers and clinical prediction tools for the evaluation of pediatric bacterial MSKIs and discuss their practical application, limitations, and integration into clinical decision-making in the emergency department (ED). Ultimately, we provide a framework to help pediatric emergency clinicians identify children who require advanced testing and interventions while avoiding unnecessary evaluation and treatment in low-risk patients.

articles.title: Oxidative stress in osteoarthritis: From mitochondrial homeostasis to targeted delivery systems.
articles.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic joint disease characterized by cartilage degradation, in which oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction play a pivotal role. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, driven by inflammation, metabolic reprogramming, and systemic risk factors, leads to mitochondrial damage, impaired mitophagy, and disrupted mitochondrial dynamics, forming a vicious cycle that accelerates OA progression. Although traditional antioxidant molecules show therapeutic potential, their rapid clearance from the joint cavity limits clinical efficacy. Recent advances in tissue engineering and smart delivery systems-such as ROS-responsive hydrogels, microspheres/nanocarriers, and exosome-based platforms-enable targeted, sustained, and on-demand drug release, offering new opportunities to restore redox balance and break the pathological amplification loop. This review systematically summarizes the molecular mechanisms linking oxidative stress to mitochondrial homeostasis in OA and highlights the design principles and application status of emerging delivery strategies, aiming to provide a theoretical foundation for next-generation precision therapies.

articles.title: Adjunct rim plating for selected pilon fracture patterns: Lessons from hyperextension tibial plateau fractures.
articles.abstract: Pilon fractures frequently involve small anterior or anterolateral marginal fragments that are susceptible to shear displacement and may not be reliably controlled by conventional periarticular plates. Rim plating is a fragment-specific, low-profile juxta-articular buttress technique that has demonstrated favorable biomechanical and clinical results in selected tibial plateau fracture patterns. This review examines the rationale for extending this concept to selected pilon fracture patterns. We performed a narrative review of clinical, cadaveric, and biomechanical studies describing rim-based constructs in tibial plateau fractures, with emphasis on hyperextension and posterolateral patterns, as well as computed tomography (CT)-based studies of pilon fracture morphology and fragment capture by precontoured plates. Relevant studies were identified through PubMed and reference screening and synthesized qualitatively to inform a technical proposal for adjunct rim plating in selected pilon fractures. The reviewed tibial plateau literature consistently identified peripheral regions that may remain unsupported by conventional periarticular plates, particularly in hyperextension and posterolateral fracture patterns, where adjunct rim plating has been associated with maintained reduction and favorable clinical outcomes. In the distal tibia, CT-based studies suggest that commonly used anatomically precontoured plates may not reliably capture the anterolateral (Tillaux-Chaput) fragment when fragment height is less than 15 mm. In this setting, an adjunct rim plate may serve as a peripheral buttress to improve support of the articular margin, distribute subchondral stress, and prevent displacement of the articular block. Rim plating may be best conceptualized as a joint-line buttress strategy for improving peripheral containment of shear-dominant marginal fragments. Extrapolation of this concept to selected pilon fracture patterns is mechanically plausible and supported indirectly by CT-based fragment-capture data. This technique may be useful in carefully selected anterior or anterolateral distal tibial rim fractures that are not adequately controlled by standard periarticular plating.

articles.title: [Acute heart failure-management during the first 120 min : Approach for early stabilization and decongestion].
articles.abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is among the most common causes of emergency department, intermediate care, and intensive care unit admission and remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in contemporary therapy. The first 120 min of management are particularly critical, as this period determines not only respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization, but also trigger identification, decongestion strategy, and the foundation for subsequent prognostic improvement. This CME article provides a practical, phenotype-based approach to the early management of AHF. The proposed strategy is centered on the rapid classification of patients according to congestion ("wet" vs. "dry") and perfusion ("warm" vs. "cold") status. Stabilization and diagnostic work-up must occur simultaneously. Early assessment should focus on identifying acute coronary syndrome, clinically relevant arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism, structural heart disease, and infectious triggers. In addition to clinical examination, electrocardiography, blood gas analysis, and biomarkers, point-of-care ultrasound with lung ultrasound and focused echocardiography play a pivotal role in the first-line evaluation. From a therapeutic perspective, early noninvasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, prompt vasodilation in hypertensive presentations, and effective decongestion with intravenous loop diuretics constitute the core interventions. In cases of insufficient response, escalation strategies such as sequential nephron blockade or selective use of vasoactive agents should be considered. Structured reassessment at short intervals is essential to detect persistent congestion, evolving hypoperfusion, inadequate therapeutic response, or overlooked differential diagnoses. The article emphasizes that successful acute management must already establish the transition toward guideline-directed long-term therapy during the first hours of hospitalization, including early initiation of evidence-based heart failure medication once hemodynamic stabilization has been achieved.

articles.title: Proximal humerus fractures: A review of current management evidence and guidance on contemporary surgical strategies.
articles.abstract: Proximal humerus fractures (PHFs) most commonly affect elderly, osteoporotic women, although younger patients sustain them through high-energy trauma. Both incidence and the associated healthcare burden continue to rise with demographic ageing. Non-operative management is preferred for undisplaced fractures and for many elderly patients, whereas a range of internal fixation methods and arthroplasty options are available for more complex injuries. Patient age, comorbidities, functional demands and fracture pattern are the primary determinants of treatment selection, implant choice and expected outcome. Absolute indications for surgery include acute fracture-dislocations, open fractures and injuries with vascular or neurological compromise. Relative indications are based on the degree of displacement and the predicted failure of non-operative treatment, and include head-splitting fractures, severe varus, valgus or posterior tilt of the humeral head, anatomical neck fractures, calcar comminution, complete displacement of the humeral head from the shaft, significant displacement of the lesser or greater tuberosity, displaced three- and four-part fractures, and large impaction defects of the humeral head, particularly when associated with instability. It is important to recognise that the displacement thresholds in routine use are pragmatic and consensus-derived rather than validated, and that expert panels do not agree on a maximum acceptable deviation. Surgery is technically demanding, requiring anatomical reduction, calcar restoration, avoidance of varus, secure fixation of the tuberosities and correct patient and implant selection. Locked plating has been the most common operation, but is associated with high complication rates and has failed to show superiority over non-operative treatment in several large randomised controlled trials. Augmentation of fixation and intramedullary nailing may address calcar comminution, metaphyseal voids and varus collapse. Arthroplasty is increasingly used in elderly patients, with reverse shoulder arthroplasty now dominating over hemiarthroplasty. Results appear better than hemiarthroplasty and plate fixation in the single trial that has compared them directly, but the evidence remains limited. To support this narrative review a systematic search was undertaken to identify every randomised controlled trial of PHF management. This review synthesises and compares current evidence on the management options for PHFs and provides practical guidance on contemporary surgical strategies.

articles.title: Management of the Critically Ill Patient with Opioid Use Disorder.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: The management of critically ill patients with opioid use disorder presents a unique challenge, as overdose, withdrawal, or concomitant intoxication, due to an unregulated drug supply, leads to physiologic changes that potentially impact standard treatment. This review article outlines an emergency medicine-focused approach for early recognition and stabilization of opioid overdose or withdrawal. Topics include naloxone, use of medications for opioid use disorder, recognition of concurrent intoxication, treatment of α2-agonist withdrawal, multimodal analgesia, and sedation for opioid-tolerant patients. The acute management of opioid use disorder is an opportunity to prevent withdrawal-related decompensation, improve comfort, and support ongoing engagement in treatment.

articles.title: The Non-invasive Hemodynamic Profile: A Modern Approach to the Evaluation and Management of Acute Decompensated Heart Failure-Related Cardiogenic Shock with Point-of-Care Ultrasound.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Emergency department presentations of acute decompensated heart failure-related cardiogenic shock (ADHF-CS) are increasing and are associated with high short-term mortality. Early diagnosis is challenging due to variable clinical presentation, compensatory physiology, and limited availability of invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Point-of-care ultrasound enables quick, noninvasive assessment of cardiac output, right atrial pressure, and systemic vascular resistance. This review outlines a practical bedside echocardiographic approach to generate a rapid hemodynamic profile in suspected ADHF-CS, facilitating accurate phenotyping and targeted resuscitation strategies in the emergency setting.

articles.title: Managing the Critically Ill Postpartum Patient in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: This review article prepares emergency physicians to recognize and manage critical illness in postpartum patients, a population at heightened risk of preventable morbidity and mortality in North America amid persistent racial/geographic disparities and shrinking obstetric access. It highlights key physiologic changes after delivery that complicate patient management. The article focuses on 3 immediate postpartum emergencies (postpartum hemorrhage, postpartum preeclampsia, and amniotic fluid embolism) and 3 subacute (pulmonary embolism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection). It concludes with system-level strategies to improve safety and outcomes.

articles.title: Refractory Shock in the Post-Cardiac Arrest Patient.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Mixed shock is common after cardiac arrest (CA), with dominant shock physiology sometimes changing over the course of hours. This article focuses on identifying dominant shock physiology in patients with refractory shock after CA and targeted strategies for resuscitation. The authors discuss approach to cardiogenic shock, including pharmacologic and mechanical support, as well as advanced pharmacologic therapies relevant to distributive shock.

articles.title: When No ICU Bed is Available: Critical Care Services in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: This review article, focused on the care of the critically ill adult when no intensive care unit (ICU) bed is available, describes current models addressing critical care services in the emergency department (ED), reviews available evidence on the impact of different approaches, and explores best practices in implementation of ED-ICU models. Based on these findings, the article explores potential benefits of leveraging the ED-ICU concept in the regional organization of critical care services.

articles.title: Titrating and Discontinuing Noninvasive Respiratory Support in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Acute respiratory failure is common in the emergency department (ED), often requiring noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS). NIRS has become a cornerstone in the initial management of acute respiratory failure. Despite its growing use, significant variability in practice remains, and evidence-based guidance specific to the ED setting is limited. This article aims to provide emergency physicians with a practical, evidence-informed framework for initiating and managing NIRS in adults with acute respiratory failure, with a focus on initial settings, titration, monitoring for failure, and guidance on weaning and liberation.

articles.title: Securing the Airway, Protecting the Brain: Neuroprotective Intubation for Acute Neurologic Emergencies.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Emergency airway management in acute brain injury carries unique physiologic risks, such as hypotension, hypoxia, hypercarbia, and sympathetic surges can precipitate secondary brain injury. This review outlines a neuroprotective approach focused on deliberate preparation, physiologic optimization, and evidence-informed techniques. Key elements include rapid ABCD assessment, recognition of elevated intracranial pressure, appropriate use of hyperosmolar therapy, strategies to blunt sympathetic surges, tailored induction and paralysis, techniques to maximize first-pass success, and postintubation ventilation and sedation aimed at maintaining eucapnia, normoxia, and stable cerebral perfusion. This approach reframes intubation as an opportunity to prevent secondary injury and improve outcomes.

articles.title: Strategies to Manage Refractory Hypoxemia in the Intubated Patient.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Persistent hypoxemia after intubation is associated with high mortality and demands a systematic approach focused on the underlying pathophysiology. This article emphasizes developing a focused differential diagnosis that includes both mechanical and patient factors to guide management. The authors review key therapeutic strategies, including careful use of positive end expiratory pressure, positioning techniques, medications such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, sedation, and neuromuscular blockade, and, when conventional therapies fail, consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

articles.title: The Architecture of Preparation: How Effective Emergency Medicine Teams Prepare for Complexity and Uncertainty.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: This article reframes preparation for critically ill patients as a dynamic, compounding process that spans 3 temporal phases: strategic, operational, and reflective. Using concepts such as shared mental models, psychological safety, adaptive capacity, and the 3A's prebriefing framework (anticipate, align, and adapt), the article outlines how teams can better navigate uncertainty and complexity in real time. This article describes the consequences of preparation deficit and preparation debt, and provide practical tactics for rapid appraisal, decision-making in motion, and structured reflection. Together, these strategies create a preparation architecture that enhances performance, reduces error, and strengthens team and system resilience.

articles.title: Emergency Burn Resuscitation: Where Evidence Meets Practice.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: The initial management of a critically ill burn patient sets the trajectory for their entire hospital course. Understanding standards of care is essential, but moving beyond rote formulas for airway management, fluids, and analgesia is critical to ensuring appropriate care and preventing iatrogenic harm. This article provides an evidence-based guide for emergency physicians on when and how to pivot from standard care to nuanced, life-saving interventions that address the dynamic pathophysiology of severe burns.

articles.title: Safely Transferring the Critically Ill Patient out of Your Emergency Department.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Regionalized systems of care increasingly rely on critical care transport (CCT) to move high-acuity patients to centers with specialized resources. This article outlines the complex clinical, operational, and ethical considerations that shape interfacility transport, emphasizing the need for deliberate risk-benefit assessment, patient optimization, and clear communication among sending clinicians, transport teams, and receiving facilities. Variability in CCT team training, capabilities, and staffing models requires clinicians to understand regional resources. By applying systems-based thinking and the "right patient, right time, right team, right place" framework, clinicians can ensure safe, equitable, high-quality transport within regionalized care networks.

articles.title: Modern Approach to Vascular Access in the Critically Ill Patient.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Vascular access is a key intervention in the management of critically ill emergency department patients. This can include peripheral or central venous access and intraosseous access. In combination with arterial catheterization, central venous access can provide key information to guide volume and vasoactive medication titration in isolation as well as in combination with dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness. This article will review the indications and contraindications as well as decision-making for the use of these modalities in light of the current evidence.

articles.title: Troubleshooting the Failed Airway.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: The failed airway is a high-stakes event arising from deranged physiology, challenging anatomy, and technical difficulty. Mitigation requires proactive resuscitation of the physiologically difficult airway and optimizing oral intubation techniques. Key procedural strategies include airway checklist use during all airways, prioritizing video laryngoscopy, employing progressive suction methods like suction-assisted laryngoscopy for airway decontamination, and using a bougie-first approach for introducer selection. When oral intubation fails, providers must be proficient in advanced techniques such as flexible bronchoscopy and emergency front-of-neck access. Simulation and continuous quality assurance are essential to maintain competency in troubleshooting the failed airway.

articles.title: Post-intubation Sedation and Analgesia in the Emergency Department: The Basics and Beyond.
articles.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Provision of postintubation sedation and analgesia is critical in emergency management of mechanically ventilated patients. Pain and sedation should be monitored using a validated scoring system, and medications titrated to a target sedation level, which should usually be light. Usually, fentanyl is the first-line analgesic and propofol is the first-line sedative. Dexmedetomidine and ketamine may be helpful in select populations, but further research is needed to define their role in the emergency department. Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided. Physicians should plan for postintubation sedation and analgesia in advance and consider using succinylcholine for intubation to avoid awareness with paralysis.

articles.title: Pediatric Patellar Injuries.
articles.abstract: Pediatric patellar injuries are common causes of anterior knee pain in children and adolescents and are frequently encountered in emergency and acute care settings. These conditions range from load-related overuse syndromes to acute traumatic injuries requiring timely recognition and referral. Unique features of the skeletally immature knee, including evolving ossification centers, open physes, and cartilaginous structures, may complicate diagnosis and contribute to missed or delayed recognition. This review provides an evidence-informed, emergency medicine-oriented approach to the evaluation and management of pediatric patellar injuries, with emphasis on key history and examination findings, imaging selection, initial treatment, and indications for orthopedic referral. Pediatric patellar conditions include patellofemoral pain syndrome, patellar subluxation and dislocation, prepatellar bursitis, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome, chondromalacia patellae, and patellar fractures. Most load-related conditions are diagnosed clinically and managed nonoperatively with symptom control, activity modification, and rehabilitation. In contrast, acute patellar dislocation and fractures require careful assessment for osteochondral injury, loose bodies, and extensor mechanism disruption. Radiographs are the first-line imaging study for traumatic presentations; magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasonography may be necessary when clinically important cartilaginous, osteochondral, or extensor mechanism injury is suspected despite nondiagnostic radiographs. Computed tomography (CT) has a selective role when detailed characterization of an osseous or osteochondral fragment would alter management. A systematic approach to pediatric anterior knee pain can help emergency clinicians distinguish low-risk load-related syndromes from injuries requiring immobilization, advanced imaging, or urgent orthopedic consultation. Attention to mechanism of injury, effusion, focal tenderness, patellar instability, and active knee extension is central to appropriate diagnosis and disposition.

articles.title: Opioid Analgesia in Acute Myocardial Infarction: Pharmacokinetic Interaction with P2Y12 Inhibitors and Pharmacodynamic Consequences-A Clinical Review for Emergency Physicians.
articles.abstract: Opioids still have a role in treating severe ischemic pain during acute myocardial infarction. Their gastrointestinal effects, however, may slow absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors and postpone platelet inhibition at a time when antiplatelet loading and percutaneous coronary intervention often occur close together. This clinical review examines the pharmacokinetic basis and pharmacodynamic consequences of the opioid-P2Y12 interaction, the uncertainty surrounding clinical outcomes, and the practical implications for emergency and prehospital care. Randomized pharmacology studies show altered early exposure to clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor after morphine, although the prasugrel effect was limited to a lower maximum active-metabolite concentration in healthy volunteers. Fentanyl also delays ticagrelor compared with no opioid, but the small head-to-head comparison with morphine was inconclusive. Trials of alternative formulations, prokinetic treatment, peripheral opioid antagonism, and opioid-sparing analgesia have largely measured drug exposure, platelet reactivity, or pain. None was powered to determine mortality, reinfarction, or stent thrombosis, and observational outcome studies remain difficult to interpret because opioid-treated patients are often sicker at baseline. In practice, pain relief should proceed alongside diagnosis and reperfusion. Nitroglycerin is appropriate when hemodynamics allow; an opioid is reasonable for severe pain that persists despite tolerated anti-ischemic therapy or when nitrates cannot be used. Small titrated doses, reassessment before redosing, and clear communication of opioid exposure, vomiting, shock, and P2Y12 loading time are more defensible than routine administration.

articles.title: Persistent postoperative hypercoagulability and venous thromboembolism risk following pelvic and acetabular fractures: A prospective pilot study.
articles.abstract: Pelvic and acetabular (PA) fractures are severe orthopaedic injuries associated with high risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), a potentially life-threatening complication, despite current thromboprophylaxis strategies. The duration of postoperative hypercoagulability and associated VTE risk following surgical fixation remain unknown. Thromboelastography (TEG) analysis can assess the entire clotting process and can be used to quantify hypercoagulability and increased VTE risk through maximal amplitude (MA) and coagulation index (CI) parameters. To characterize the extent and duration of postoperative hypercoagulability and VTE risk following PA fractures using serial TEG analysis. Adults undergoing surgical management of PA fractures were prospectively enrolled. Serial TEG analysis was performed from admission to 3 months postoperatively. Standardized thromboprophylaxis consisted of low-molecular-weight heparin for 28 days postoperatively. Screening compression ultrasound was performed to detect asymptomatic proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT) on postoperative day 3 (POD3). Mobility was measured using Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. One-sample t-tests compared mean MA and CI values at each time point with predefined hypercoagulable thresholds (MA ≥65 mm, CI >3). Thirty patients were enrolled, including 22 men (median age: 52.5 years). Most were hypercoagulable by POD3 and MA peaked on POD7. Hypercoagulability persisted in 75.0% and 38.5% of patients at four and six weeks, respectively. At three months, 28.6% remained hypercoagulable. 23.3% developed VTE (five pulmonary emboli, two proximal DVTs). Patients with acetabular fractures had consistently higher MA values. Despite standard thromboprophylaxis, patients with PA fractures demonstrated persistent hypercoagulability and a substantial VTE rate. These findings suggest that thrombosis risk may persist beyond current thromboprophylaxis durations and support further investigation of individualized strategies, particularly following acetabular fractures.

articles.title: A structured three-step reduction strategy for locked posterior fracture-dislocation of the proximal humerus through a standard deltopectoral approach: A retrospective case series.
articles.abstract: Locked posterior fracture-dislocation of the proximal humerus is a rare and technically demanding injury in which the humeral head remains impacted posterior to the glenoid. Although several reduction techniques have been described, the practical details of anterior-only reduction remain incompletely standardized. We evaluated a structured three-step anterior reduction strategy performed through a standard deltopectoral approach. We retrospectively reviewed 16 consecutive patients with acute locked posterior fracture-dislocation of the proximal humerus treated between January 2016 and January 2022. All patients underwent reduction through a single deltopectoral approach followed by locking-plate fixation supplemented with suture fixation. The reduction strategy consisted of (1) establishing an anterior reduction corridor by opening the anterior joint through an L-shaped subscapularis incision or a lesser-tuberosity fracture interval, (2) guiding the humeral head with a periosteal elevator introduced between the humeral head and glenoid, and (3) unlocking and translating the head anteriorly using gentle elevator assistance, controlled arm rotation, and, when head-shaft control was limited, direct digital manipulation. Outcomes included fracture union, avascular necrosis (AVN), recurrent dislocation, implant-related complications, range of motion, Constant-Murley score, and subscapularis function. The mean age was 41.1 ± 8.4 years. The mean interval from injury to surgery was 3.4 ± 1.0 days. All 16 reductions were completed through the initial deltopectoral approach without an additional posterior incision, conversion to arthroplasty, or intraoperative complication. Mean operative time was 85.9 ± 10.5 min and mean estimated blood loss was 152.5 ± 27.7 mL. All fractures achieved radiographic union during available follow-up. At a mean follow-up of 21.2 ± 9.4 months (range, 12-48 months), the mean Constant-Murley score was 85.4 ± 8.6 (range, 70-96). Mean forward flexion, abduction, extension, and external rotation were 151.6 ± 22.7°, 135.0 ± 29.9°, 29.4 ± 10.0°, and 38.1 ± 4.8°, respectively. Internal rotation ranged from T7 to L4. Using the descriptive thresholds applied in the original study (excellent, ≥90; good, 80-89; fair, 70-79), 5 patients were excellent, 8 good, and 3 fair. No AVN, recurrent dislocation, implant-related complication, deep infection, or reoperation was observed during the available follow-up. Lift-off and bear-hug tests were negative in all patients at 12 months. This series supports a structured, reproducible anterior-only reduction strategy for selected acute locked posterior fracture-dislocations of the proximal humerus. The principal contribution is the standardization of the reduction sequence and the description of how the humeral head can be disengaged and translated without a posterior approach. The technique should not be interpreted as a wholly novel reduction maneuver, and the absence of AVN should be interpreted within the available follow-up period. Level IV; Therapeutic study.

articles.title: Delirium in burn patients: Incidence, risk factors, and management strategies.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness, and cognition. Delirium is common and multifactorial in pediatric and adult burn patients. Delirium can be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed in phenotype. This is an important complication associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased morbidity and mortality, and possibly long term cognitive and psychological sequelae, highlighting the importance of prevention and early recognition. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable due to the combination of the intense systemic inflammatory response, disruption of the blood brain barrier, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter imbalances, and impaired cerebral energy metabolism involved, not to mention the frequent painful procedures, heavy sedation and analgesia requirements, and inherent risks of critical illness and ICU admission themselves. This review summarizes the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic challenges, management, and prevention of delirium in burn patients, highlighting issues specific to this population.

articles.title: Lawyers in the burns unit - a review of pro bono legal services provided for patients with burn injury.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: We present a review of a pro bono legal service provided to patients treated at a regional burns centre in the United Kingdom for the period between October 2012 and October 2019. A solicitor, supported by a paralegal, was available to give pro bono advice to any patient attending the burns service. The legal team provided assistance to patients and their relatives with advice pertaining to their personal and financial affairs as impacted by the injury. This was provided independently from, but in addition to, existing support from the hospital legal and ethical departments. The pro bono legal service has advised on 108 patient cases since this service began in October 2012 and has provided more than 2100 h of solicitors' time. 777 h were spent on non-compensation advice given on welfare benefits and insurance. Advice on welfare and/or financial matters was requested by all patients, and although potential claims for compensation against a third party were found in 83 cases, of these, the law firm operating the legal service was known to have been instructed to pursue recourse in only 16 cases. However, of the 16 cases instructed to make a compensation claim so far, 6 cases have settled, recovering a total of over £ 3.7 million. This review shows a likely benefit to patients from pro bono legal advice available in a burns unit setting. It also showed the significant financial gain to the government and potentially the NHS when a compensation claim was made by a patient.

articles.title: [Measures to improve bystander resuscitation : Kids Save Lives and public-access defibrillation].
articles.abstract: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and early use of automated external defibrillators (AEDs) are key measures to improve neurologically intact survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). In Germany, however, heterogeneous emergency medical service structures, insufficient legal frameworks for public-access defibrillation, and only partially implemented CPR training in schools limit the full realization of this potential. This review summarizes the available evidence on school-based CPR training, national and international programs (including "Kids Save Lives"), and innovative mobile AED strategies. As an example, a regional project in the city and district of Osnabrück is presented, in which a non-profit organization has been implementing CPR training in schools since 2020, training both teachers and students. Building on this, regional initiatives have been launched to systematically record and improve the availability of AED locations. Based on these findings, key fields of action for policymakers, emergency medical service providers, and civil society stakeholders are identified. Nationwide, legally mandated CPR training in schools, a structured public-access defibrillation concept including AED registries, and the consistent involvement of local non-profit organizations appear crucial to strengthening the early links in the chain of survival and to sustainably improving outcomes after OHCA.

articles.title: [Prehospital point-of-care ultrasound (pPOCUS): "See, decide, act" : Evidence, training concepts, and the role of pPOCUS in the acute assessment of traumatic and nontraumatic emergencies].
articles.abstract: Prehospital point-of-care ultrasound (pPOCUS) enables focused sonography for immediate management-relevant clinical questions. To summarize the role of pPOCUS in traumatic and nontraumatic emergencies with regard to evidence, indications, training, and limitations. pPOCUS may provide clinically relevant adjunctive information in trauma, acute dyspnea, chest pain, undifferentiated shock, resuscitation, and selected procedural settings. Current evidence supports its feasibility and frequent impact on management decisions, whereas robust data on patient-centered outcomes remain limited. The clinical benefit of pPOCUS depends on appropriate indications, integration into team workflows, structured training, documentation, and quality assurance. pPOCUS should be regarded as focused decision support rather than as an exclusionary diagnostic modality.

articles.title: [Chemical attacks and accidents : Prehospital management].
articles.abstract: Chemical attacks and accidents involving so-called C (chemical)-agents are rare but represent a significant challenge for emergency medical services. More often than classical warfare agents, "dual-use" substances used in industry and everyday settings are involved. Early recognition of a possible exposure is crucial, for example, through clustering of cases or unexplained symptom patterns consistent with a toxidrome. Simple interventions such as undressing and dry decontamination can substantially reduce contamination and help with patient and personnel safety. Initial medical management follows ABCDE (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure) principles and may be supplemented by targeted antidote therapy. Knowledge of the clinical features, key problems, and management of common substance groups such as organophosphates or cyanides enables a structured and effective approach and is discussed in this article.

articles.title: Skin grafting and regeneration: Bridging biological barriers towards functional regeneration.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Despite being the clinical gold standard of care for severe skin defects, autologous grafting is constrained by limited donor resources, associated morbidity, and incomplete functional recovery. These challenges have catalyzed a transition toward regenerative approaches that seek holistic restoration of cutaneous structure, physiological function, and psychosocial well-being. Significant hurdles persist, notably an imbalanced regenerative microenvironment leading to scarring, immune rejection limiting graft survival, and inadequate vascularization and innervation hampering functional integration. Translational challenges further include limited model validity, complex scalable manufacturing, difficulties in long-term efficacy verification, and cost-related accessibility issues. To overcome these obstacles, next-generation strategies are converging on three key approaches. The first is seed cell reprogramming, such as the use of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). The second involves smart biomaterials combined with advanced fabrication techniques like 3D bioprinting to generate pre-vascularized grafts. The third is the spatiotemporally controlled delivery of bioactive factors. The future points toward intelligent, personalized systems where electronic skin (E-skin) enables real-time monitoring and artificial intelligence (AI) supports risk prediction and implant design via multi-omics data. Realizing this vision will require deep integration across disciplines, alongside adaptive regulatory and reimbursement frameworks. This narrative review aims to summarize current advances in skin grafting and regenerative strategies, with a particular focus on the biological barriers that limit functional skin regeneration and the emerging approaches developed to overcome them.

articles.title: Toxic epidermal necrolysis: Management in the ICU.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Epidermal necrolysis (EN) includes Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS, detached/detachable skin surface <10% body surface), toxic epidermal necrolysis (EN, detached/detachable skin surface ≥30%), and SJS-EN overlap (detached/detachable skin surface 10-29%). These are rare but severe cutaneous adverse reactions, usually triggered by drugs. Drugs account for 85-90% of cases, with onset typically 4-28 days after exposure. The acute phase is life-threatening, with respiratory and septic complications being the main determinants of prognosis. Mortality averages 15-20%. Supportive care is the cornerstone of management. Any suspected drug should be stopped as soon as possible. No immunomodulatory treatment has been shown to be effective in halting detachment, or reducing mortality. Multidisciplinary management should take place in specialized centers led by dermatology teams. This review article aims at reviewing the current knowledge on the management of EN in the intensive care unit during the acute phase, in expert centers -eventually burn centers- including supporting care and pharmacological interventions.

To cradle or not: assessing the use of a lumbar puncture cradle on lumbar puncture success rates.
articles.abstract: Neonatal and infant lumbar puncture success rates range from 50 to 80%, while traumatic lumbar punctures are reported in 30-50%. A novel lumbar puncture cradle, SMöLTAP®, designed to standardize seated positioning may improve procedural outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the first-pass success and traumatic lumbar puncture rates using the cradle compared to the lateral decubitus. This was a single-center cohort study from August 2020-October 2024 in a tertiary pediatric emergency department. Term and corrected preterm infants (≥ 37 weeks, ≤ 3 months) requiring a lumbar puncture were identified through an EPIC report. Unstable infants, those requiring opening pressure, performed under sedation or using ultrasound guidance, and charts with missing documentation were excluded. Lumbar punctures using the cradle were identified first, and a stratified random sampling technique was used to select the non-exposed cohort, in which lumbar punctures were performed in the lateral decubitus position. Chi-square analysis and logistic regression were used to analyze lumbar puncture success rates. 142 infants were included (mean age 26 days, 57% male). Cradle use was associated with a higher first-pass success rate: 63%, as opposed to 41% in the control lateral decubitus group p = 0.01. It remained significantly associated with first-pass success after a multivariable logistic regression (OR 2.23, 95% CI 1.06-4.68, p = 0.03). Cradle use was associated with fewer traumatic lumbar punctures, 36% versus 59% (p = 0.01), percent difference 23% (95% CI 6.6-37.8). There was no difference in the overall success rate, 80% versus 70%, p = 0.17. The cradle is a promising tool that may improve first-pass success, reduce traumatic lumbar punctures, and provide more precise management of febrile infants requiring a lumbar puncture, thereby reducing clinical diagnostic and management challenges.

articles.title: A Retrospective Study of the Efficacy of Regional Anesthesia in Reducing Donor Site Harvest Pain in Burn Patients.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Despite advances in burn care, the pain of burn treatment remains unresolved. The creation of donor harvest sites is often unavoidable, and the subsequent pain is difficult to treat. Regional anesthesia for the donor harvest sites can provide effective analgesia, however, there is limited literature regarding its efficacy. The purpose of this study was to assess the use of regional anesthesia for donor harvest site pain. Patients admitted to the burn center from January 1, 2011, to May 15, 2025, with thigh donor site harvest(s) were reviewed for study inclusion. Data collected included demographics, burn variables, hospital course data, and regional anesthesia procedure details. Descriptive statistics were used to determine differences between the block and non-block groups. Of the 524 patients included, 164 (31.3%) had donor site blocks and 360 (68.7%) did not. There were 77 (47%) with single shot blocks and 87 (53%) had indwelling catheters (groin or epidural). The groups were well-matched in their demographics, burn injury data, and hospital variables. The overall oral morphine equivalents (OME) and pain report levels were similar between the block and control groups in all three post-operative periods. However, causal conclusions are limited by this retrospective, heterogenous study. An appropriately protocolized prospective study is planned.

articles.title: Transanal irrigation to treat refractory constipation: a short-term real-life study.
articles.abstract: The treatment of patients complaining of chronic constipation is still far from ideal, and there is a discrete percentage of them that are labeled as refractory to the usual therapeutic approaches. In these patients there is often the need to use alternative approaches. Among these, transanal irrigation seems promising. Our aim was to evaluate the effect of transanal irrigation on symptoms and quality of life in patients with severe refractory constipation. To this end, we retrospectively analyzed the charts of 31 such patients undergoing transanal irrigation, and evaluated them basally and one and three months after the treatment. Data were collected by means of the Wexner score and the SF12 questionnaire for quality of life. Overall, there was a significant decrease of the constipation scores and an improvement of quality of life score after treatment, after both one and three months. No important side effects were documented. In conclusion, treatment with transanal irrigation may be useful, alone or as combination therapy, in patients with constipation refractory to the conventional therapeutic approaches, but studies in more numerous cohorts of subjects are needed to firmly validate this approach.
