articles.title: The Impact of Dyschromic Burn Scar on Satisfaction with Appearance: A Burn Model System Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Advances in acute burn care have substantially improved survival, shifting focus toward long-term complications of burn injury that affect quality of life. Hypertrophic scarring is common after burn injury and is often accompanied by dyschromia, a change in scar pigmentation relative to uninjured skin. Despite its visibility, the psychosocial impact of postburn dyschromia remains poorly characterized. This study examined the relationship between dyschromia, scar thickness, and satisfaction with appearance in burn survivors using longitudinal data from a large, multicenter cohort. Data were obtained from participants enrolled in a national longitudinal burn outcomes database (Burn Model System) with follow-up through 24 months after hospital discharge. Dyschromia and the presence of raised or thick scar were assessed by patient self-report, and satisfaction with appearance was measured using a validated self-report scale. Multivariable logistic regression, survival analyses, and mixed-effects models were used to evaluate cross-sectional and longitudinal associations. Dyschromia was highly prevalent at discharge and strongly associated with raised or thick scar. Female sex and scar thickness were independently associated with reporting dyschromia. Among participants who identified as Black, raised or thick scar predicted both the presence of dyschromia and delayed resolution over time. Persistent dyschromia was associated with sustained dissatisfaction with appearance, while resolution of dyschromia coincided with improvements in satisfaction with appearance. Across models, scar thickness emerged as a consistent determinant of poor psychosocial outcomes. These findings highlight dyschromia as a clinically meaningful sequela of burn injury that is closely linked to fibrotic scar pathology and long-term satisfaction with appearance.

articles.title: Staged Biodegradable Temporizing Matrix and Meek Micrografting as a Donor-Sparing Strategy for Extensive Burn Injuries.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Definitive closure of extensive burns remains constrained by donor-site availability, particularly in patients with burn injuries of 50% total body surface area (TBSA) or greater. Biodegradable Temporizing Matrix (BTM) can stabilize excised wounds while donor sites recover, whereas Meek micrografting permits controlled expansion of limited autologous skin. We retrospectively reviewed adult patients admitted between May 2022 and May 2025 with burns of 50% TBSA or greater who underwent BTM application followed by Meek micrografting as part of definitive wound closure. Demographic, injury, operative, and outcome variables were collected from electronic medical records, operative reports, anesthesia records, wound-care documentation, and clinical photography. Twelve patients were included. Mean age was 41.5 years, mean burn size was 63.1% TBSA, and mean Baux score was 104.6. All patients had inhalation injury and required tracheostomy. Biodegradable Temporizing Matrix was applied at a mean of 13.3 days after admission, and Meek micrografting was performed at a mean of 42.2 days. Mean TBSA covered by Meek micrografting was 32.5%, representing 50.6% of the total burn surface. Operative efficiency improved from 15.2 to approximately 10.8 min per 1% TBSA covered over the study period. Clinically documented Meek graft take exceeded 90% in evaluable cases, no patient required secondary autografting of Meek-grafted BTM areas, and 11 of 12 patients survived to discharge or inpatient rehabilitation. Staged BTM followed by Meek micrografting is a feasible donor-sparing strategy for extensive burn closure that permits special-area prioritization, donor-site recovery, and efficient definitive coverage of large prepared wound surfaces.

articles.title: Incident-Reporting and Severity-Weighted Safety Learning in an Adult Regional Burn Center: A Five-Year Review.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Voluntary incident-reporting systems are widely used in hospitals, but their value depends on classification quality, review processes, linkage to complementary safety pathways, and translation into learning. Burn centers are vulnerable to fragmented safety intelligence because care spans resuscitation, critical care, surgery, wound management, rehabilitation, reconstruction, and outpatient follow-up. We reviewed institutional incident reports assigned to an adult regional burn center from April 1, 2021, to March 31, 2026. The dataset contained 1418 reports. The most frequent categories were specimen or laboratory events; medication or fluid events, safety, security, or miscellaneous events; and pressure injuries. Harm level was not visible in structured form in 811 reports (57.2%). This absence was patterned: 546 of 547 specimen or laboratory reports and all 130 pressure-injury reports lacked visible structured harm classification. Pressure-injury stage or category was not reliably available in the analytic extract and was not imputed as a surrogate for harm. Among 607 reports with specified harm level, 16 were moderate and 4 severe. Severity-weighted review changed interpretation: infection prevention and control accounted for only 17 reports overall but 14 of 20 moderate or severe harm reports. Narrative follow-up was present in most high-harm reports, but structured contributing factors were absent in 17 of 20. Incident reporting should be one input into a severity-weighted burn-center learning system with harm classification at review or closure, escalation, action ownership, implementation resources, documented closure, and feedback to frontline teams.

articles.title: Effect of a Preoperative Communication Checklist on Operative Efficiency in Burn Surgery: A Quality Improvement Analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Preoperative communication checklists are used to improve surgical safety and team coordination. We evaluated whether introduction of a preoperative communication checklist was associated with reduced operative duration in a burn operating room. We conducted a quality improvement (QI) study comparing operative outcomes before and after introduction of a preoperative communication checklist in a burn unit. Cases from August 19, 2020, to August 20, 2022, were included, with checklist introduction occurring on August 20, 2021. Adult patients undergoing excisional debridement procedures were analyzed. The primary outcome was operative duration. Mixed-effects models were used to assess the association between checklist use and operative duration while adjusting for surgeon, procedure type, and square area excised. A total of 139 patients undergoing 281 operations were included (143 pre-checklist, 138 post-checklist). Mean operative duration decreased from 107.8 minutes pre-checklist to 96.0 minutes post-checklist. In adjusted analysis, checklist use was associated with a 17.99-minute reduction in operative duration (P < .001). Procedures involving autograft, ReCell, and biodegradable temporizing matrix were associated with increased operative time, as was greater square area excised. In interaction models, the overall reduction was not statistically significant; however, ReCell procedures demonstrated a significant reduction of 30.49 minutes (P = .003) following checklist introduction. Introduction of a preoperative communication checklist was associated with decreased operative duration. The greatest effect was observed in ReCell procedures, suggesting that improved preoperative coordination may enhance efficiency in complex workflows. Preoperative checklists represent a scalable QI strategy to optimize operative efficiency and resource utilization in burn care.

articles.title: Inpatient Complications and Outcomes for Burn Patients Admitted with Opioid-Positive Drug Screens.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Opioid use disorder complicates the management of burn injuries, particularly in achieving adequate pain control. While prior single-institution studies have evaluated associations between opioid use and burn outcomes, multi-institutional analyses of inpatient complications remain limited. Using the American Burn Association Noncommercial Burn Research Dataset, this study compares inpatient outcomes among patients with prehospital opioid-positive screening versus those with negative screening. Among 32 052 patients included, 50.5% screened positive for opioids at the time of presentation. These patients were more likely to be female (P < .0001), more likely to possess scald injuries (P < .0001), and less likely to be experiencing homelessness (P < .0001) or to be diagnosed with inhalation injury (P < .005). Opioid positivity was associated with increased odds of infectious complications, such as cellulitis (OR = 2.7, P < .0001) and sepsis (OR = 1.41, P < .001). Opioid negativity, conversely, had a higher prevalence of acute respiratory distress syndrome (P < .0001), acute kidney injury (P < .0001), respiratory failure (P < .05), and cardiac arrest (P < .05). The opioid-negative population also necessitated more frequent admission to the critical care unit (P < .05) and demonstrated higher overall mortality (P < .0001). These findings highlight the vulnerability of opioid-negative patients who may have delayed presentation and more severe injuries than originally anticipated. This work underscores the need for heightened vigilance and equitable, early care for these patients to mitigate risk in this group.

articles.title: Multicenter Analysis of Standard of Care Versus Oxandrolone Versus Testosterone in Burn HypermetaboliSm (MASCOTS).
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Severe burn injury results in a profound hypermetabolic state that complicates management and recovery. Oxandrolone has historically been used to help attenuate this response, but its withdrawal from the United States (US) market has led to increased use of alternative anabolic agents such as testosterone and human growth hormone (HGH). However, studies comparing the efficacy and safety between these alternative anabolic agents in adult burn patients remain limited. In this multicenter study, patients were stratified based on if they received testosterone, oxandrolone, HGH, or no anabolic supplementation. Baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes were analyzed with analysis of variance and Chi-square testing as appropriate. Propensity score matching was used to adjust for baseline differences in injury severity and patient characteristics. 813 patients who sustained major burn injuries between June 2022 and June 2025 across 12 verified US burn centers were analyzed. Anabolic supplementation was not associated with improved inpatient weight maintenance when compared with no anabolic supplementation (P = .064), nor with differences in median weight change. Patients receiving anabolic therapy experienced longer hospital and intensive care unit stays (P = .026). Overall mortality did not differ between treated and untreated patients (P = .885); however, mortality was higher among patients treated with oxandrolone compared with testosterone (P = .001). Anabolic therapy was associated with higher rates of venous thromboembolic events (P = .019). These findings underscore that optimizing anabolic therapy will require balancing efficacy, safety, and economic considerations, with a focus on long-term functional outcomes beyond initial hospital stay.

articles.title: Predictors of Response to Fractional CO2 Laser Therapy in Hypertrophic Burn Scars: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Hypertrophic burn scars are associated with significant functional impairment and psychosocial morbidity. While fractional CO₂ laser therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving scar quality and symptoms, limited data exist on how baseline scar characteristics and patient factors influence treatment response. This study evaluated whether baseline scar severity, total body surface area (TBSA), and duration of initial hospital stay predict responsiveness to fractional CO₂ laser therapy, and whether laser treatment is associated with a reduced need for scar contracture release procedures. A retrospective cohort study was conducted including patients with burn injuries who underwent fractional CO₂ laser therapy. Scar severity was assessed using the Vancouver Scar Scale (VSS) before and after treatment. Additional variables included TBSA, length of initial hospitalization, and incidence of subsequent scar contracture release procedures. A control cohort of patients with burn injuries who did not receive laser therapy was included for comparison. Statistical analyses were performed to identify predictors of scar improvement and associations with procedural outcomes. Baseline VSS score was the strongest predictor of treatment response, with higher initial severity associated with greater improvement following laser therapy. Total body surface area and hospital length of stay were not significantly associated with treatment response. Laser therapy was associated with fewer scar contracture release procedures; however, this did not reach statistical significance, likely due to limited sample size. These findings suggest initial scar severity is a key determinant of laser responsiveness and support further study in larger cohorts.

articles.title: Anesthetic Practices for Laser Therapy in Pediatric Patients With Hypertrophic Burn Scars: A Retrospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Burn injuries are a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, disproportionally impacting pediatric patients. Many affected children will develop hypertrophic scarring, limiting activity, restricting range of motion, and negatively impacting psychosocial development. Although laser therapy is a routine treatment for hypertrophic burn scars in children, there is no consensus on the best anesthetic technique. In this multicenter retrospective cohort study, we aimed to identify effective anesthetic strategies that correlated with outcomes for pediatric laser scar therapy. We characterized perioperative anesthetic approaches for pediatric patients with burn scars who were undergoing laser therapy at 2 academic centers from 2020 to 2023. Among 239 encounters for 98 patients, intraoperative/postoperative opioids were given in 53% of encounters. Preoperative opioid use was associated with 86% lower odds of intraoperative/postoperative opioid administration (OR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.06-0.34; P < .001). A 2-fold increase in total body surface area treated was associated with a 32% increase in the odds of opioid use (OR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.11-1.58; P = .002) and 23% greater odds of pain (OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.05-1.43; P = .009) when controlling for other variables. Laser type was associated with a 2-fold higher odds of pain (OR, 2.11; 95% CI, 1.07-4.14; P = .030), and the incidence of emergence delirium was low (2.5% of the cohort). Differences in laser type and anesthetic management also varied across institutions, which impacted pain and recovery. These findings uncovered key patient and procedure factors that can inform standardized anesthetic guidelines for pediatric laser scar therapy.

articles.title: Identifying Risk Factors for Inpatient Falls in Burn Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Inpatient falls are associated with prolonged hospital stays, increased complications, and substantial economic burden. Burn patients face unique risks due to impaired mobility. Yet, risk factors and outcomes in burn units remain underexplored. This retrospective cohort study evaluated the impact of inpatient falls on adult burn outcomes. Predictors of fall risk to guide prevention strategies were identified. Adult patients admitted for burn injuries from January 1, 2015, to July 31, 2024 were included. Fallers were identified through an internal auditing system and matched 1:2 to non-fall controls based on age, sex, TBSA, and inhalation injury. Demographics, comorbidities, medication use, Fall Risk Assessment Score (FRAS), physical and occupational therapy assessments, and fall safety measures were collected. Univariate, receiver operating characteristic curve, and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed; P < .05 was considered significant. One hundred thirty-two patients were included, 45 fallers and 87 non-fallers. Fallers were more likely to use antihypertensives (62.2% vs. 39.1%, P = .016) and antiarrhythmics (75.6% vs. 52.9%, P = .014) than non-fallers. They required greater mobility assistance at admission (Basic mobility score 16 [11.3-20] vs. 20 [14-24], P = .002). Fallers required more help for activities of daily living (Daily activity score 16 [12-19] vs. 19 [14-22], P = .004). The FRAS predictive value was moderate (AUC = 0.653, P = .009). Burn surgery requirement (odds ratio (OR) = 3.35 [1.12-10.1], P = .031) and FRAS (OR = 1.12 [1.04-1.20], P = .003) were independently associated with fall risk. These findings underscore the value of functional assessment and proactive, tailored fall prevention.

articles.title: Residential Air Pollution, Inhalation Injury, and Burn Recovery: A Burn Model System Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Chronic air pollution, specifically particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), increases the risk and severity of acute respiratory distress syndrome and is most concentrated in lower-income areas. Burn survivors from these communities may be especially vulnerable to respiratory complications of burn injury and inhalation injuries. In this retrospective national longitudinal cohort study of adult burn survivors (2015 and 2021), the association of 3-year pre-burn PM2.5 exposure, estimated from home census-tract code from the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Network of the Center for Disease Control (CDC), and clinical outcomes extracted from the Burn Model System (mortality, ventilator days, tracheostomy, hospital length of stay (LOS), and patient-reported outcomes from Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Global Health and employment status at 6 and 12 months) were assessed via mixed-effects regression models adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, total body surface area, and inhalation injury (IH). Among 582 adult burn survivors (mean age of 46.2 years), unadjusted models found that higher PM2.5 exposure was associated with longer LOS, worse Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Global Health scores (pooled 6 and 12 months), and a decreased likelihood of employment at follow-up (pooled 6 and 12 months). These associations were attenuated after adjustment; though PM2.5 exposure was associated with IH, which was strongly associated with prolonged ventilation, tracheostomy, lower Global Health scores, and lower employment at follow-up. Higher PM2.5 exposure was associated with a greater likelihood of IH, which was associated with poorer outcomes, suggesting that residential PM2.5 exposure, or factors that co-vary with it, may identify patients at greater risk for IH and poorer recovery after burn injury.

articles.title: Reviewing the Safety of Providing Out-of-Operating-Room Anesthesia for Acute Burns in Pediatric Patients.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Pain management is a cornerstone of acute pediatric burn care, and burn wound care frequently requires sedation or anesthesia to optimize patient comfort and procedural success. Anesthesia delivered outside of the operating room (OR) has been shown to be a safe and effective alternative to OR-based care; however, eligibility has traditionally been restricted to older and larger children. Following a quality care audit in 2022, eligibility for anesthesiologist-administered out-of-OR anesthesia at our tertiary pediatric burn center was expanded to include children aged 8-12 months and/or weighing 8-10 kg. The objective of this study was to compare key quality and safety indicators between patients meeting expanded eligibility criteria and those meeting historical criteria (>10 kg and/or 12-24 months) undergoing burn dressing changes in a general anesthesia-ready satellite anesthesia room. This single-center retrospective study included patients treated between January 2022 and January 2024. Outcomes included procedure duration, anesthetic technique, airway management, anesthesia-related complications, and postprocedure disposition. A total of 211 patients undergoing 296 procedures were included. Burn characteristics were similar between groups, with scald injuries and partial-thickness burns predominating. No episodes of oxygen desaturation, hemodynamic instability, airway obstruction, or difficult mask ventilation were observed. One episode of laryngospasm occurred in the expanded group and resolved with conservative airway management. Procedure duration was shorter, while time to discharge was slightly longer, in the expanded group. These findings suggest that expanding eligibility criteria for out-of-OR anesthesia in pediatric patients with burn injuries is safe and feasible, without compromising procedural efficiency or outcomes.

articles.title: Serial Casting as a Conservative Treatment for Adults With Upper Extremity Burn Contractures: A Prospective Longitudinal Study With a Criterion for Change.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Joint contractures and hypertrophic scars (HSc) are common complications following burn injuries, significantly impairing range of motion (ROM) and quality of life. While conservative interventions target either contractures or HSc, serial casting (SC) is typically reserved for patients who fail traditional therapy or are nonadherent. The purpose of this study was to estimate the extent to which ROM (regular and revised passive and active), scar characteristics (objective and subjective), and patient-reported upper extremity (UE) function change following an individually tailored SC treatment program after switching from a minimum of 3 days of usual care. This study employed a prospective longitudinal intervention design with a criterion for change. Participants with UE joint passive ROM (PROM) loss of > 15% were included. Measures were taken at baseline, pre-SC, every Monday and Friday thereafter, and 3 weeks after casting. The QuickDASH and Patient Scar Assessment Scale were evaluated at baseline and 3 weeks after casting. Eleven individuals (13 joints) were included in this study. Regular PROM, revised PROM, and active ROM and scar thickness improvements were statistically significant. Participants reported improvements in UE function for 11/13 joints (median 16%, range 9%-21%) and scar impression for all scars (median 6, 4-10). Participants also perceived that SC reduced their rehabilitation burden. In conclusion, when possible, SC should be prioritized to increase PROM, reduce HSc thickness, and enhance patient-perceived UE function and scar outcomes.

Association of tranexamic acid with early death or massive transfusion after severe pelvic ring fractures: A nationwide registry-based cohort study.
articles.abstract: Evidence for tranexamic acid during emergency treatment of severe pelvic ring fractures is limited. We examined its association with early death or massive transfusion. We studied adults in the Japan Trauma Data Bank from 2019 to 2023 with blunt pelvic ring fractures of Abbreviated Injury Scale severity 3 or higher. Exposure was any in-hospital tranexamic acid. The primary outcome was death within 24 h after arrival or transfusion of at least 20 Japanese red blood cell units within 24 h after injury. We used multiple imputation, propensity-score overlap weighting, and hospital-clustered standard errors. Among 5288 patients, 1985 (37.5%) received tranexamic acid. The weighted primary-outcome risks were 13.0% with tranexamic acid and 18.1% without it (risk ratio 0.72, 95% confidence interval 0.60-0.87). The association was driven by 24-hour mortality (risk ratio 0.62, 95% confidence interval 0.48-0.80); massive transfusion alone (risk ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.73-1.21) and mean red blood cell use did not differ. Any red blood cell transfusion was more frequent with tranexamic acid (risk ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.11-1.30). The primary-outcome risk ratio was 0.76 (0.62-0.93) after excluding deaths within 2 h and 0.81 (0.65-1.00) when both components were assessed within 24 h after injury. The mortality association was not accompanied by lower transfusion requirements and weakened when outcome time origins were aligned. Because treatment timing was unavailable, these findings do not establish an independent survival benefit and provide no corroborating transfusion evidence of a pelvic-specific hemostatic benefit.

articles.title: Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes in patients with severe pelvic ring injury requiring REBOA: A two-center matched cohort study.
articles.abstract: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized. This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up. Forty-nine REBOA-treated patients were matched 1:1 to 49 non-REBOA patients by major Young-Burgess category, Injury Severity Score, and age. The primary outcome was functional status among hospital survivors, categorized as good/fair/poor. Deep surgical site infection (SSI) after definitive pelvic fixation was the key secondary outcome, and nonunion was exploratory. Main models used a propensity-score linear predictor based on age, Injury Severity Score, initial systolic blood pressure, and lactate. Seventy-five patients survived hospitalization (30 REBOA; 45 non-REBOA); median follow-up was 19 months. Good/fair/poor outcomes were 16.7%/46.7%/36.7% in REBOA survivors and 51.1%/37.8%/11.1% in non-REBOA survivors. REBOA exposure was associated with worse functional status after adjustment (common odds ratio [cOR], 3.14; 95% CI, 1.11-8.92; P = 0.032). Among 68 definitive-fixation survivors, deep SSI occurred in 44.0% versus 9.3% (adjusted OR, 7.01; 95% CI, 1.88-31.07; P = 0.003); all observed events occurred within 60 days. Nonunion occurred in 26.7% versus 6.7% (adjusted OR, 9.09; 95% CI, 2.00-53.71; P = 0.004). Sensitivity analyses for deep SSI were directionally consistent. Among hospital survivors, REBOA exposure was associated with poorer long-term functional recovery and a higher burden of deep SSI. Nonunion was more frequent but remained exploratory. These findings characterize a high-risk orthopaedic survivor phenotype but do not establish a direct causal effect of REBOA.

articles.title: Impact of sarcopenic obesity phenotype on long-term survival in geriatric trauma: A nationwide cohort study using weight-adjusted waist index.
articles.abstract: As the global population ages, identifying effective prognostic markers for elderly trauma patients has become crucial. While Body Mass Index (BMI) is commonly used, its utility is limited by the "obesity paradox," failing to differentiate between muscle and fat. This study aimed to evaluate the Weight-Adjusted Waist Index (WWI), a surrogate marker for sarcopenic obesity, as a predictor of 20-year mortality following heavy trauma in the elderly. We analyzed a nationwide cohort of 18,366 elderly patients (age≧65) from the National Health Insurance Service-National Sample Cohort (NHIS-NSC) who experienced heavy trauma (hospitalization, surgery, or ICU admission) between 2002 and 2022. Patients were categorized into WWI tertiles. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for 20-year mortality, adjusting for demographics, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and laboratory findings. During the 20-year follow-up, the highest WWI tertile (T3) was associated with significantly higher mortality compared to the lowest tertile (T1). In the fully adjusted model, the HR for 20-year mortality in the T3 group was 1.72 (95% CI 1.55-1.91). Notably, the risk was more pronounced in obese patients (BMI≧25 kg/m2, HR 2.15) and those with low physical activity. Furthermore, high WWI was associated with a higher prevalence of hip and femur fractures (26.0% vs. 15.0%) and prolonged ICU stays. WWI is a superior and independent predictor of long-term mortality compared to BMI in elderly trauma patients. By effectively identifying the high-risk sarcopenic obesity phenotype, WWI provides a practical and powerful tool for risk stratification in geriatric trauma management.

articles.title: Should Esophageal Temperature Probes Be Used within UK Search and Rescue Helicopter Services?
articles.abstract: Due to the environment in which they operate, UK search and rescue helicopters (SARH) may encounter patients presenting with accidental hypothermia or hypothermic cardiac arrest. For these patients, accurate core temperature measurement allows thorough assessment of hypothermia severity and determines the recommended clinical interventions and conveyance decisions. Ongoing monitoring of core temperature also provides feedback to clinicians on the effectiveness of rewarming interventions. Currently, SARH paramedics use peripheral thermometers, which some evidence suggests may not be appropriate for assessing hypothermic patients in this environment. The implementation of esophageal temperature probes (ETPs) may allow clinicians to meet the needs of a wider range of patient presentations. This article aims to discuss the demand, practicality, and training required to implement ETPs into SARH paramedic practice and highlights an opportunity for further research.

articles.title: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting - A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture.
articles.abstract: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous ECG recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide. Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27.2% (standard deviation 30.5%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22.0 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0.0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (p = 0.031). During TCP, clinicians verbalized a palpable pulse 26 times across 19 patients. Only 4 instances (15%) coincided with electrical capture. Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

articles.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions.
articles.abstract: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors. We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates. Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%). Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

articles.title: Prognostic value of the red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio in alcohol-related sarcopenia.
articles.abstract: Chronic alcohol consumption is associated with sarcopenia, a metabolic disorder characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass and function. The red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio (RAR) has emerged as a composite biomarker reflecting inflammation, oxidative stress, and nutritional status. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of RAR in patients with alcohol use disorder and sarcopenia. We conducted a prospective observational study including 231 patients with chronic alcohol consumption (mean intake 200 g/day) recruited at a tertiary hospital between 2008 and 2025. Clinical, analytical, and body composition variables were assessed using densitometry and handgrip strength. Probable sarcopenia was defined according to EWGSOP2 criteria based on low muscle strength. Cox and logistic regression models and ROC curve analysis were performed. RAR was positively associated with liver dysfunction and inflammatory markers, and inversely correlated with appendicular lean mass and handgrip strength. In patients with probable sarcopenia, RAR was independently associated with 12-month mortality (hazard ratio 1.67; 95% confidence interval 1.32-2.11; p < 0.001). The predictive capacity of RAR was high (AUC 0.81; 95% CI 0.67-0.94). In conclusion, RAR is a simple, low-cost, and independent prognostic biomarker that integrates inflammatory and nutritional status in patients with alcohol use disorder and sarcopenia.

articles.title: Fixation of patellar fractures using bioabsorbable hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide cannulated screws and subperiosteal nonabsorbable sutures.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Bioabsorbable implants offer a promising alternative to metallic fixation for patellar fractures, potentially avoiding hardware-related complications. In 2023, a new generation of bioabsorbable hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide (HA/PLLA) cannulated screws was introduced, featuring a low-profile (2 mm) trident-shaped head and increased root diameter for enhanced strength. This study evaluates the clinical outcomes of a surgical technique combining these redesigned screws with subperiosteal nonabsorbable sutures. Between April 2023 and May 2025, 19 consecutive patients with transverse patellar fractures (AO/OTA 34-C1/C2) underwent open reduction and internal fixation. Two bioabsorbable cannulated screws were used. High-strength nonabsorbable sutures were passed through the screw channels and a central bone tunnel using a double-loop sliding knot for compression. The sutures were systematically routed subperiosteally to minimize tissue irritation. Full weight-bearing with a brace began on postoperative day one. Clinical and radiographic outcomes were assessed. This study was approved by the institutional review board of Kainan Hospital. The mean maximum articular surface gap was 8.7 ± 5.2 mm. The mean follow-up was 8.6 ± 3.0 months. Bone union was achieved in all cases. At the final follow-up, the mean knee flexion was 138.7° ± 13.0° and extension was - 1.6° ± 3.4°. No postoperative complications, including infection, loss of reduction, screw breakage, or symptomatic hardware irritation, were observed during the follow-up period. No reoperations were required during the follow-up period. All patients achieved bone union. No major complications or reoperations were observed during the follow-up period. These preliminary findings suggest that this technique may be feasible for transverse patellar fractures.

articles.title: Beyond Dialysis Independence: The Importance of Longitudinal Renal Follow-Up after Severe Acute Kidney Injury.
Emergency Department-Administered Extended-Release Buprenorphine After Fentanyl Overdose Reversed by Emergency Medical Services With Naloxone.
articles.abstract: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers are on the frontline of the opioid epidemic and administered naloxone to reverse suspected overdose over 442,000 times in 2024. Interest in EMS-initiated sublingual (SL) buprenorphine (BUP) exists; however, initiation of month-long extended-release buprenorphine (XR-BUP) in the immediate postoverdose period has not yet been described. The high risk of death from repeat overdose in patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) could be reduced by administration of XR-BUP. The purpose of this case report is to highlight the utility of EMS-initiated SL-BUP followed by XR-BUP to potentially improve care linkage and adherence to medication-assisted OUD treatment. A bystander call to 911 dispatched a Basic Life Support (BLS) unit to an unresponsive 30-year-old man found with fentanyl-smoking paraphernalia. First responders administered 8 mg of intranasal naloxone. Paramedics arrived 8 min later and assessed the patient to be in opioid withdrawal with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 22. The patient reported using heroin or fentanyl and methamphetamine daily. After consent, paramedics administered 16 mg of SL-BUP. In the ED, an addiction medicine consult service administered a 300-mg monthly XR-BUP formulation. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: We report that rapid transition from naloxone reversal of overdose and EMS initiated SL-BUP to month-long XR-BUP is possible during a single emergency medicine encounter using a stepwise clinical pathway. We hope our observations encourage further prospective study of the intervention described as this may link patients to medication assisted OUD treatment, which decreases mortality in patients with OUD.

articles.title: Massive Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in an Adolescent Patient: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in pediatric patients arises from diverse etiologies that vary across age groups. Although it is an uncommon cause of life-threatening hemorrhagic shock, prompt recognition and management are essential. Owing to the infrequency of hemorrhagic shock from GI bleeding in pediatrics, emergency physicians may lack familiarity with its diagnosis and management. Furthermore, multiple etiologies may coexist and may not be detected during the initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy, increasing the risk of premature diagnostic closure. A 17-year-old boy with a history of plaque psoriasis was transported by ambulance to the pediatric emergency department of an urban level one trauma center, presenting with copious hematemesis and hemodynamic instability. Initial resuscitation in the emergency department included blood transfusion, followed by admission to the pediatric intensive care unit. The first endoscopic evaluation by pediatric gastroenterology identified duodenal erosion; however, the patient experienced further large-volume bleeding out of proportion to these findings. A subsequent endoscopy revealed a Dieulafoy lesion, which was treated successfully. The patient was ultimately discharged home and has remained stable during long-term follow-up. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: Although severe GI bleeding in pediatric patients is uncommon, emergency physicians must quickly identify hemorrhagic shock across all age groups and be familiar with the broad differential diagnoses that vary by age. Initial management must prioritize airway protection and hemodynamic stabilization as a bridge to definitive intervention. Clinicians should recognize the limitations of endoscopic gastroduodenoscopy and consider the potential for concurrent sources of bleeding that may necessitate additional intervention. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. articles.title: Transanal Extrusion of Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Tubing in a Pediatric Patient.
articles.abstract: Gastrointestinal perforation is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts. Patients may have minimal or no abdominal symptoms despite bowel perforation and the risk of ascending central nervous system infection. A 12-year-old boy with hydrocephalus treated with a VP shunt presented to the Emergency Department after his parents discovered a segment of rubber tubing in his stool. He was afebrile, well appearing, neurologically at baseline, and without abdominal pain, vomiting, or symptoms of shunt malfunction. His abdominal examination was benign. A shunt series demonstrated an intact right-sided VP shunt and retained catheter fragments from a previously disconnected left-sided shunt, without an apparent abnormality of the functioning shunt. Despite the reassuring examination and radiographic findings, passage of shunt tubing per rectum raised concern for bowel perforation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, and urgent surgical exploration demonstrated that the functioning right-sided VP shunt had perforated the colon with formation of a fistulous tract. The shunt was externalized and the colonic defect repaired. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures subsequently grew gram-negative organisms, requiring complete shunt removal, external ventricular drainage, and prolonged antimicrobial therapy.Why Should an Emergency Physician Be Aware of This?: Transanal extrusion of VP shunt tubing should prompt immediate concern for bowel perforation even in an asymptomatic, well-appearing patient with reassuring initial imaging. Prompt recognition, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, and urgent neurosurgical and surgical consultation are essential because bowel perforation may permit ascending infection resulting in ventriculitis, meningitis, or sepsis.

articles.title: Real-Time Ultrasound Guided Paramedian Lumbar Puncture in the Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: Pediatric lumbar puncture is often performed using the traditional landmark approach. The ultrasound-assisted approach has demonstrated benefit, but its efficacy is limited by the lack of real-time ultrasound needle guidance. The ultrasound-guided paramedian technique is a novel approach that allows for active ultrasound guidance of the needle into the spinal canal. We describe 2 cases of successful ultrasound-guided paramedian lumbar puncture in the pediatric emergency department.

articles.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors in Geriatric Heart Failure: Evidence, Safety, and Clinical Implementation.
articles.abstract: This review summarizes the rationale, efficacy, safety, and implementation of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in older adults with heart failure (HF). SGLT2i have become an integral part of contemporary HF therapy, with benefits demonstrated across the ejection fraction spectrum. Age subgroup analyses from randomized trials, frailty analyses, meta-analyses, and real-world cohorts suggest that benefits on HF hospitalization and cardiovascular outcomes are largely preserved in older and frail patients. Observational data in patients aged  ≥ 75 and > 80 years further support potential effectiveness in very old and multimorbid populations. However, geriatric vulnerability modifies clinical implementation, particularly regarding volume status, renal function, risk of falling, genitourinary infections, nutritional status, cognition, polypharmacy, and self-care capacity. Available evidence suggests that SGLT2i remain effective and are generally well tolerated in older patients with HF. Older age alone should therefore not preclude SGLT2i therapy. In geriatric HF, treatment decisions should be individualized according to frailty, comorbidity burden, safety risks, functional status, self-care capacity, and goals of care.

articles.title: Development and validation of methods to predict ground- and helicopter-based emergency medical service travel times.
articles.journal: Scandinavian journal of trauma, resuscitation and emergency medicine
articles.abstract: Helicopter-based Emergency Medical Services (EMS) are a costly and finite resource and should only be deployed when they provide substantial benefits to patients. One such benefit is a more rapid response to incidents and transport to hospital compared to Ground-based EMS. This study evaluates methods for estimating travel times for the purpose of optimizing the selection of helicopter vs. ground EMS. Ground EMS travel times were estimated using an open-source routing tool, the estimates of which were adjusted using linear regression and gradient boosting models based on historical travel times. Helicopter travel times were similarly estimated based on great circle distances adjusted by historical data. Models were evaluated using several measures of predictive accuracy to enable comparison with other studies. In validation data collected after finalization of the methods, the best performing prediction models for Ground EMS travel times explained a substantial portion of variation in drive times to location and to hospital (R2 0.79 and 0.70 respectively), and less for helicopter flight times (R2 0.46 and 0.38 respectively). Mean average percentage error was 18-20% for all investigated estimation techniques and time intervals. Integrating tools based on the open-source code provided with this study has the potential to improve the ability of dispatchers to estimate relative travel times and assess the potential time benefit of directing the most appropriate resources to a given patient.

articles.title: Evaluation of early hydrocortisone use for hemodynamic shock in adult burn patients with suspected critical illness related corticosteroid insufficiency.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI) presents as refractory hemodynamic shock in critically ill patients. Research on CIRCI and its treatment in burn patients is limited. We sought to review the use of corticosteroids in a burn population during their first week of hospitalization. The burn registry and the electronic medical records were queried for burn patients admitted between January 2015 and December 2025. The following variables were abstracted: demographics, burn history, hospital course, and treatments. Outcome variables included length of stay (LOS), infections, graft loss, pharmacological treatment, and mortality. The two groups were compared with Student's T-test and Chi Square where appropriate. A multivariant analysis was performed to determine independent predictors of CIRCI, infection and mortality. Significance was determined at p<0.05 level. The study group consisted of 87 patients in hemodynamic shock receiving vasopressors, with 47 also receiving corticosteroids. The corticosteroid group had larger burns (37.6 v 25.1%), more resuscitation (15.9 v 8.1 L), more vasopressor days (6.23 v 3.7 d), more ventilator days (19.72 v 7.83 d), more infections (66% v 34%) and longer LOS (51.53 v 26.05 d), all p<0.05. On multivariant analysis, variables independently related to the diagnosis of CIRCI were age and resuscitation fluids; to infection were corticosteroid use; and to mortality were age. Overall, over 50% of patients in hypotensive shock during their first week of treatment were diagnosed and treated with corticosteroids for suspected CIRCI. More study is needed to determine the appropriate role of corticosteroid use in early burn treatment.

articles.title: When emergency medicine isn't there: a scoping review of global acute care substitutes and complements for disaster response and surge capacity.
articles.abstract: Disasters and everyday gaps in emergency care force acute illness and injury to be managed outside of formal emergency medicine (EM) and emergency medical services (EMS) systems. Because EM capacity varies substantially worldwide, this scoping review applies a substitutes-and-complements framework to the mechanisms that deliver acute care in and around formal EM or EMS, classifying their roles as substitutes, complements, or both across levels of EM system maturity and disaster conditions. The resulting typology serves as an inventory of latent disaster surge capacity. Following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, five databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and CINAHL) were searched, yielding 11,161 records. After title and abstract screening, 758 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility and 115 studies were included. We charted study type, country, and EM system maturity, using a codebook derived from American College of Emergency Physicians' (ACEP) International Ambassador country reports, the primary acute-care mechanism, care-delivery context, and COVID-19 relevance. Mechanisms were then classified by whether they substituted for or complemented formal EM. Publications were concentrated in the COVID-19 era (82/115, 71% from 2020 or later) and in high-income, mature-EM settings (United States 30%; 64/115 mature-EM). The most common mechanisms were lay and community first-responder programs (n = 18), hospital-at-home and remote monitoring (n = 15), and telehealth-based emergency and behavioral-health services. Overall, substitutes predominated (75/115), whereas complements (18/115) clustered in mature-EM systems. Our inventory of latent surge capacity reframes each mechanism as a potential candidate for transfer across the EM-maturity spectrum: routine substitutes used in low-maturity systems may offer pre-planned crisis capacity for mature systems, while lower-infrastructure telehealth models may provide decision support or partial substitution where formal EM is limited. The substitute-complement balance tracks maturity, but the opportunity lies in translating mechanisms to the settings where they are not currently used as such.

articles.title: Osteoporosis treatment gaps and risk of recurrent hip fracture following initial fragility fracture: Insights from over one million cases.
articles.abstract: Patients who sustain a hip fracture are at high risk of a second hip fracture, yet most do not receive osteoporosis pharmacotherapy. We evaluated the association between bone-health medication initiation after a first hip fracture and the risk of a second hip fracture. This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, a de-identified multi-institutional electronic health record database. Adults who underwent surgery for a first femoral neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric hip fracture were classified as having no bone-health medication, as baseline users (medication documented at admission), or as initiators within six months of the index fracture. Second hip fracture was assessed over fixed 1-, 2- and 5-year horizons. We estimated absolute risks, cumulative incidence accounting for death as a competing risk, and multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models. Overall, 1,051,020 patients were eligible for the 5-year analysis: 705,059 (67.1%) had no medication, 83,452 (7.9%) were baseline users and 262,509 (25.0%) initiated medication within six months. Five-year cumulative incidence of second hip fracture was 17.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.1-17.3) with no medication, 14.1% (95% CI 13.8-14.4) among baseline users and 8.9% (95% CI 8.8-9.1) among initiators. In adjusted models, the hazard of second hip fracture was lower among baseline users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71, 95% CI 0.69-0.73) and initiators (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.37-0.39) than among patients with no medication. Initiation of bone-health medication within six months of a first hip fracture was associated with a lower risk of a second hip fracture. Baseline users had intermediate risk, which may reflect confounding by indication, agent selection or adherence. These findings support early, coordinated post-fracture osteoporosis treatment; the observational design precludes causal inference.

Effect of Rescuer Position on Chest Compression Quality and Rescuer Stability during CPR on a Sloped Surface: A Simulation Study.
articles.abstract: IntroductionHigh-quality chest compressions (CCs) are essential for survival after cardiac arrest. Current cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) guidelines recommend performing CCs on a firm and flat surface; however, cardiac arrest may also occur in austere environments such as mountainous or sloped terrain where such conditions cannot be achieved. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of rescuer positioning on CC quality during CPR on a slope.MethodsA repeated-measures simulation study was conducted with 50 basic life support-trained volunteers. Participants performed uninterrupted CCs for 2 min in 3 different positions relative to the victim on a natural slope: uphill, downhill, and parallel. CC quality was assessed using a Resusci Anne QCPR manikin and the Laerdal QCPR application.ResultsRescuer position significantly affected CC quality and subjective ratings (P < 0.05). The downhill position achieved the highest proportion of time within the recommended compression rate range (median 90% vs 30% in the uphill position; P < 0.001) and deeper compressions (71 mm vs 67 mm; P < 0.001). In contrast, the uphill position was associated with higher compression rates and reduced chest recoil quality. Subjective assessments also differed significantly between positions. Compared with the downhill position, the uphill position was associated with greater physical demand, poorer stability, increased hand slipping, and greater fear of falling (all P < 0.001).ConclusionsRescuer position significantly influences CC quality and perceived rescuer safety during CCs on sloped terrain. Performing CCs from a downhill position may improve CC performance in austere and mountainous environments.

articles.title: Biphasic Biochemical Pattern Suggestive of Second-Wave Muscle Injury in Exertional Rhabdomyolysis.
articles.abstract: BackgroundExertional rhabdomyolysis is an important cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in otherwise healthy individuals following strenuous physical activity. Serum creatine kinase (CK) typically peaks within 24 to 72 h and progressively declines with appropriate supportive management. A secondary biochemical rise after initial improvement is uncommon and may reflect ongoing skeletal muscle injury.Case PresentationA 21-year-old previously healthy man presented with severe generalized myalgia, dark-colored urine, and progressive oliguria progressing to anuria following a prolonged trekking expedition. Initial investigations revealed severe rhabdomyolysis with a CK of 18,500 U/L, dialysis-requiring AKI (serum creatinine 9.0 mg/dL), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis, and myoglobinuria. Intermittent hemodialysis was initiated because of severe AKI with persistent anuria and metabolic complications. Serial biochemical monitoring initially demonstrated improvement; however, on the fourth hospital day, an unexpected secondary rise in CK (14,900-22,600 U/L) occurred, accompanied by recurrent hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, worsening metabolic acidosis, and increased AST and LDH, despite ongoing renal replacement therapy. This biphasic biochemical pattern was considered suggestive of delayed or "second-wave" skeletal muscle injury. The patient received a total of 5 hemodialysis sessions with continued supportive care, following which urine output progressively improved, biochemical abnormalities resolved, and renal function recovered completely.ConclusionThis case highlights a rare biphasic biochemical pattern in severe exertional rhabdomyolysis, characterized by a secondary surge in muscle injury markers and metabolic abnormalities after initial improvement. Recognition of this potential "second-wave" phenomenon emphasizes the importance of continued serial CK and biochemical monitoring in patients with severe rhabdomyolysis.

articles.title: Operational end-of-life trajectory categories among patients who died in the emergency department: associations with resuscitative and palliative care in a five-year retrospective cohort.
articles.abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) increasingly care for patients approaching the end of life, yet the relationships between patterns of decline and final ED care remain poorly characterised. The objective was to describe the distribution of retrospectively assigned trajectory-oriented categories among ED decedents and examine associations with care processes. This single-centre retrospective cohort study included adults who died in the ED between 2018 and 2022. Categories were acute event/low comorbidity (T1), terminal malignancy or pre-existing exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care (T2), advanced chronic disease with acute decompensation (T3), frailty/dementia or high comorbidity with severe functional dependency (T4), and residual unclassified cases (T5). Primary outcomes were CPR and documented initiation of exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care; documented end-of-life recognition or discussion was secondary. Of 628 patients, 1.3% were T1, 10.8% T2, 10.0% T3, 49.4% T4, and 28.5% T5. CPR ranged from 75% in T1 to 24% in T2 and T4 (p<0.001). Exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care was initiated in 35% of T2 and 11% of T3-T5 patients (p<0.001). End-of-life recognition or discussion ranged from 12% in T1 to 51% in T2 (p=0.034). Frailty and dementia represented the main trajectory of death in the ED, while nearly one-third of patients could not be classified within the predefined categories. A pragmatic trajectory-oriented framework may help interpret observed patterns of care. However, retrospective assignment and the large residual group make these findings hypothesis-generating; prospective validation is required before decision-support use.

Easy as 1-2-3! Point-of-Care Ultrasound Estimation of Parapneumonic Effusion Size Using Intercostal Spaces in the Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: There is limited evidence on the ability of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to quantify and characterize pediatric parapneumonic effusions. This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between lung POCUS and radiology ultrasound (RADUS) or chest x-ray (CXR) in determining effusion size and complexity in children presenting to the pediatric emergency department (ED). We studied patients aged younger than 18 years diagnosed with parapneumonic effusions at the Hospital for Sick Children between June 1, 2018, and December 1, 2024. Included patients had undergone a lung POCUS demonstrating a pleural effusion and a RADUS or CXR within 36 hours of their POCUS examination. Patients with suboptimal POCUS images were excluded. Using previously described criteria, we determined whether an effusion was "drainable" or "non-drainable" using the number of involved intercostal spaces as an estimate of effusion size. Our primary outcome was the rate of agreement between the POCUS estimation of effusion size to that of RADUS (or CXR if RADUS was unavailable) using Cohen Kappa statistic. We also compared the rate of agreement between POCUS and RADUS for effusion complexity and the time taken to complete both imaging modalities. Eighty-five cases were included in this study. POCUS agreed with RADUS substantially in its ability to quantify (κ=0.76) and characterize (κ=0.65) parapneumonic effusions. There was also substantial agreement between POCUS and CXR for estimating effusion size (κ = 0.71). The median time to complete POCUS was significantly shorter compared with RADUS (6 vs. 14 min; P=0.003). Using a simple method of counting involved intercostal spaces, our results support the use of lung POCUS for quantifying and characterizing parapneumonic effusions in the pediatric ED. Future research is needed to evaluate the generalizability of these findings and their impact on clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Comment on "Challenging the Paradigm: Fascia Iliaca Blocks May Not Be Necessary for All Neck of Femur Fractures".
Corrigendum to "Proximal humerus fractures: A review of current management evidence and guidance on contemporary surgical strategies" [Injury 57(11) (2026) 113748].
Single crash, multiple stories: A finite mixture perspective of motorcycle injury severity with a focus on post-crash medical, rescue, human and roadway-environmental factors.
articles.abstract: This study investigates the factors, including post-crash medical conditions (i.e., Glasgow Coma Score "GCS", Systolic Blood Pressure "SBP"), emergency response (i.e., pre-hospital time and mode of evacuation), human factors, and roadway-environment, affecting the Injury Severity Score (ISS) in motorcycle crashes. Utilizing a comprehensive hospital-based dataset in Karachi, Pakistan, and after addressing the issues of missing or inappropriate values via synthetic data generation, a Tobit regression (baseline) model was first employed in a corner solution setup. Harnessing 204,503 hospital-based motorcycle crash records (2007-2015) from Karachi (Pakistan), missing and inappaorpirate values were addressed through synthetic data generation. A baseline model and a finite mixture Tobit model (accounting for unobserved heterogeneity) were employed. The findings from the baseline model indicate that compared to mild/normal GCS (13-15) and SBP (> 89 mmHg), for crash victims with severe GCS (3-8) and severely low SBP (2-49 mmHg), the ISS significantly increases by 4.5249 and 7.8042 units, respectively. A positive non-linear association between prehospital time (PHT) and ISS was established. The baseline model recognizes over-speeding, nighttime crashes, wrong-way riding or driving, and involvement of multiple vehicles to significantly increase ISS by 0.1909, 0.0198, 0.0787, and 0.3333 units, respectively. The finite mixture Tobit model identifies two latent classes of crash victims with dissimilar ISS patterns and varying relationships of key correlates with ISS, indicating that reliance on a standard Tobit model could lead to misleading inferences. The practical implications are discussed in the paper.

articles.title: Harnessing the potential of response surface methodology-based optimized scaffolds in volumetric muscle loss repair in sprague dawley rat.
articles.abstract: Volumetric Muscle Loss (VML) is a complex tissue injury characterised by loss of tissue beyond the body's intrinsic regenerative capacity, resulting in impaired muscle regeneration and functional recovery. Limited cellular proliferation and poor in situ healing make VML one of the most challenging issues in tissue engineering. Conventional approaches of acidic gelling and use of artificial substrates compromise the structural integrity, biocompatibility and functional performance of tissue-engineered constructs. Moreover, the irregular geometries of muscle defects make surgical reconstruction technically challenging and often insufficient to achieve complete functional restoration. In this study, a novel porous scaffold containing collagen, fibronectin, and raloxifene (a cell-proliferative drug) was prepared for VML repair. The concentration of scaffold components was optimized using Response Surface Methodology (RSM) to obtain an effective scaffold composition. The regenerative efficacy of the optimized scaffold was evaluated in a Sprague-Dawley rat model of VML. The results suggested that RSM-optimized scaffold significantly improved VML repair after 21 days (p < 0.05) in vivo. A prominent development of muscle fibre and deposition of collagen was observed. At molecular level, a significant increase in the expression of MyoD and STAT3 genes was observed in optimized scaffold group, suggesting enhanced myogenesis and tissue repair. The findings indicate that RSM may be utilized to optimize the tissue-engineered construct to improve VML repair.

articles.title: General anesthesia is associated with increased postoperative morbidity and mortality in frail patients undergoing hip fracture fixation.
articles.abstract: Anesthetic management of hip fracture fixation has two primary modalities: general anesthesia (GA) and spinal anesthesia (SA). Choice of anesthesia often depends on institutional protocols and the individual anesthesiologist, due to a lack of consensus guidelines. Most studies have conflicting evidence and focus primarily on elderly age as a risk factor, without accounting for frailty. This study investigates whether frailty influences the relationship between anesthetic modality and postoperative outcomes. This retrospective study queried the ACS-NSQIP from 2015 to 2020 for patients who underwent hip fracture fixation with open reduction internal fixation with plate and screws or intramedullary implant insertion. Patients were separated based on whether they received GA or SA. Frailty was evaluated using the 5-Item Modified Frailty Index (mFI-5). Patients classified as frail or severely frail were included. Multivariable regression adjusting for age, sex, ASA classification, smoking, and the comorbidities significant on univariate regression was performed. The outcomes examined were mortality, unplanned readmission, and overall complications within 30 days postoperatively. This study included 24,401 patients under GA and 6193 patients under SA. On multivariable regression analysis, GA was independently associated with increased odds of mortality, unplanned readmission, and all complications among frail patients. Severely frail patients under GA had increased odds of unplanned readmission and all complications. When looking at both frail and severely frail patients together, GA remained a significant predictor of mortality, unplanned readmission, and all complications. After controlling for ASA classification, our study found that frail and severely frail patients undergoing GA for hip fracture fixation had significantly increased odds of mortality, unplanned readmission, and all complications. Our findings suggest that SA may be safer compared to GA in frail patients undergoing hip fracture fixation. Frail patients that undergo GA may benefit from increased postoperative monitoring to help mitigate complications.

articles.title: Tele-Resuscitation in Prehospital Care: Expanding Remote Guidance.
Comparative study of autologous bone graft and bone morphogenetic protein-2 for bone regeneration using a novel rabbit Masquelet technique model.
articles.abstract: The Masquelet technique is widely used for reconstructing critical-sized bone defects; however, autologous bone grafting (ABG) is associated with donor-site morbidity such as pain and bleeding. Bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) has attracted attention as a potential alternative strategy for promoting bone regeneration. Studies on direct comparisons between BMP-2 and autologous bone grafting within the context of the Masquelet technique are limited. The purpose of this study was to establish a novel rabbit femoral Masquelet model and compare the bone regenerative capacity of ABG with β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) loaded with BMP-2. A 20-mm segmental defect was created in the femur of 24-week-old New Zealand White rabbits and stabilized with a locking plate. The defect was filled with polymethyl methacrylate cement, which was removed four weeks later to induce membrane formation. The defect was subsequently filled with autologous iliac bone (ABG group) or β-TCP granules containing BMP-2 (BMP-2 group). Bone regeneration was evaluated 12 weeks after the second surgery using radiographic, histological, micro-computed tomography (μCT), and biomechanical analyses. Radiographic evaluation demonstrated satisfactory bone union in both groups, without substantial difference in union rate. Histological analysis showed cortical continuity and new bone formation in both groups. μ-CT revealed that the bone volume/tissue volume ratio of total calcified callus was significantly higher in the ABG group, whereas the tissue mineral density was significantly higher in the BMP-2 group. Biomechanical testing showed no significant differences in ultimate stress, extrinsic stiffness, or failure energy between the two groups. In this rabbit femoral Masquelet model, BMP-2 delivered with β-TCP achieved bone regeneration comparable to that of autologous bone grafting. These findings suggest that BMP-2 may represent a promising option for bone reconstruction using the Masquelet technique.

articles.title: Bacterial cellulose-sericin gold nanoparticle conduit functionalized with GDNF for peripheral nerve regeneration: An experimental sciatic nerve injury model in rats.
articles.abstract: Although the application of autografts continues to be regarded as the gold standard for the treatment of peripheral nerve injuries, there exists a necessity for alternative grafting materials. This study investigates the effects of a nerve conduit obtained from bacterial cellulose (BC) membranes modified with gold nanoparticles (AuNP) and functionalized with the GDNF neurotrophic factor on repair in peripheral nerve injury. Bacterial cellulose membranes obtained from Gluconacetobacter xylinus cell culture were modified with sericin-gold nanoparticles produced by green synthesis and functionalized with glial-derived neurotrophic factor to become conduits. A unilateral 8 mm sciatic nerve defect was created in Wistar rats (n = 21). Rats were divided into three groups as autograft (n = 7), BC-AuNP (n = 7), and BC-AuNP/GDNF (n = 7). Gait analysis and electromyography (EMG) measurements were performed at the end of the 8th week. Tissues from the sciatic nerve were obtained for histological and immunohistochemical analysis. By the result of the 8th week, the BC-AuNPs/GDNF group attained results comparable to those of the autograft group, as indicated by the sciatic function index derived from gait analysis and EMG measurements. Examinations of axon diameters, myelin sheath thickness, and vessel count demonstrated that the autograft and BC-AuNPs/GDNF groups exhibited significantly elevated values in comparison to the BC-AuNPs group. In the management of peripheral nerve injury, the application of BC-AuNP/GDNF yielded healing outcomes that were comparable to those achieved through autograft, both functionally and histologically.

articles.title: How have management and outcomes of periprosthetic proximal femoral fractures changed? A comparison of two 8 year time periods in a high volume centre.
articles.abstract: Periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFFs) are now the leading cause of major reoperation following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Patients are often frail and surgeries increasingly complex. We reviewed PFFs over two consecutive 8-year periods to analyse trends in incidence, management and outcomes to assess the evolving clinical and service impacts. A retrospective review was conducted using data from the Fracture Outcomes Research Database (FORD) and the National Hip Fracture Database (NHFD) across two 8-year periods (2007-2015 and 2016-2024). Radiographic and clinical records were reviewed. Fracture classification, management, comorbidities and mortality were recorded and compared. A regression analysis was performed to determine co-morbidities that significantly increased the risk of 12-month mortality. In the 2016-2024 period, data on re-operations rates were recorded. PFF increased from 189 to 320 across the two periods, totalling 509 patients. The incidence of Vancouver B2 fractures increased more than 1.5x, rising from 42/189 (22.2%) to 117/320 (36.6%) patients. Fixation remained the most common treatment across the two periods (75.1% and 63.4%), while revision arthroplasty was performed in 22.8% and 18.4% respectively. B2 fracture management changed significantly with fixation increasing (59% v 9.5%; p < 0.001) and revision arthroplasty rates decreasing (38.5% vs 85.7%; p < 0.001). Time to theatre improved (5-3.7 days; p = 0.028) and a higher proportion of patients returned to their pre-injury residence (30.2%; 57/189 vs 39%; 96/320, p = 0.068). No difference in mortality was observed at 30 days (2.6-3.1%; p = 0.796) or 90 days (5.8% vs 9.1%; p = 0.233) but mortality was higher at 12 months (12.2-20%; p = 0.028). ASA 4 patients increased (14%; 25/179; vs 29.1%; 82/282, OR = 2.526 (95% CI 1.54-4.14), p < 0.001). Re-operation rates were lower in the fixation group than in the revision group (12; 5.9% vs 8; 13.6%; p = 0.095). The incidence and mortality associated with PFFs are rising within our unit, despite improved time to theatre and improved discharge outcomes. This trend may reflect a frailer cohort with higher ASA grades. We demonstrate a shift in practice, with more B2 fractures treated with fixation, achieving good outcomes suggesting fixation may be a safe treatment option in selected frail patients.

articles.title: Profound motorcycle risks: a national mileage exposure-adjusted analysis.
articles.abstract: Motorcycle crashes (MCC) account for a minority of vehicle miles in the United States, but their exposure-adjusted burden among trauma admissions is not well defined. The purpose of this study was to compare the injury burden of MCC versus motor vehicle crashes (MVC) using outcomes standardized by annual vehicle miles traveled (VMT). A retrospective cohort study of American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs (ACS-TQP) admissions from 2017 to 2023 was performed for adults aged 18-80 years admitted after MCC or MVC. Primary outcomes were admission, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, amputation, and in-hospital mortality per 100 million VMT using Federal Highway Administration denominators. Motorcycle VMT was used for MCC, and light-duty vehicle VMT was used for MVC. Secondary outcomes included Injury Severity Score thresholds (≥16 and ≥25), severe head/neck injury, open long-bone fracture, ventilation, and return to the operating room. Relative risks (RRs) were estimated using binomial regression models with a log link. Among 1,419,094 admissions, 334,310 followed MCC and 1,084,784 followed MVC. MCC accounted for 23.6% of admissions but only 0.71% of included VMT. Per 100 million VMT, MCC had higher rates of admission (236.4 vs. 5.49; rate ratio, 43.0), ICU admission (70.8 vs. 1.57; rate ratio, 45.1), amputation (5.06 vs. 0.028; rate ratio, 183.0), and in-hospital mortality (6.4 vs. 0.12; rate ratio, 51.6). Among admitted patients, MCC was associated with higher risks of open long-bone fracture (14.7% vs. 6.6%; RR, 2.22), amputation (2.1% vs. 0.5%; RR, 4.25), and in-hospital mortality (2.7% vs. 2.2%; RR, 1.20). MCCs contribute a disproportionately high burden of severe trauma in the United States, with higher mileage-adjusted rates of ICU admission, amputation, and in-hospital mortality than MVCs.

articles.title: Prognostic factors and visual outcomes in badminton-related ocular injuries: A retrospective study.
articles.abstract: To evaluate a large cohort of eye patients from India for the epidemiology, clinical presentation, and visual outcomes of ocular injuries sustained while playing badminton. Medical records of patients presenting with badminton-related ocular injuries were reviewed to compare the predicted visual outcome with that stipulated by the Ocular Trauma Score (OTS). The patients' data on demographics, mode of injury, clinical evaluation, and treatment modalities were compiled, analysed and interpreted to contrast alongside OTS, the standardised prediction of visual outcomes after indexing the severity of eye injury. A total of 486 patients were included. Blunt trauma from being hit by badminton shuttlecock was the most common mechanism, followed by racquet injury, and spectacle injury. Closed-globe injury was predominant (97.33%). None of the players were using protective eyewear. Visual prognosis was generally favourable in closed-globe injury (mean final BCVA 0.32 ± 0.56 logMAR) compared to open-globe injury (0.46 ± 0.68 logMAR). Significant predictors of visual outcome included presenting BCVA, early post-injury BCVA, cataract, secondary glaucoma, optic disc involvement, iridodialysis, and OTS. OTS categories 3-5 showed better visual outcomes than predicted by the original OTS model. Closed-globe injury represented the most common injury in badminton-related ophthalmic trauma.
